title: RLVR is a Kernel, Not a Function: Statistical Inference for pass@𝑘 Crossovers

paper.title: RLVR is a Kernel, Not a Function: Statistical Inference for pass@ k k Crossovers
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) often improves
pass@1 while falling behind its base model at larger sampling budgets k k ,
a crossover read as evidence that RLVR only sharpens existing capability.
We identify two limits to this reading. First, a visible crossing need not
be statistically established: comparing models on the same prompts, we
build confidence bands across sampling budgets k k that require evidence
of both an early gain and a later loss. Across five public RLVR pairs no
crossing is statistically established in the initial evaluations, while a
32k-token evaluation on fresh prompts locates a reversal with first loss
between 11 and 61 samples; power analysis shows why failure to detect a
crossing need not mean no crossing, and why more prompts can help more
than more answers per prompt. Second, base success alone does not
determine what RLVR does to a prompt: prompts with the same base success
rate have different post-RL success rates, and these differences repeat
across independent generation halves. The relationship is a conditional
distribution—a Markov kernel—rather than a single curve, and fitting
it predicts crossings in independent generations for the same prompts and
corrects the simple model’s power estimates. Theory further shows how
losses on a minority of the hardest prompts can overturn an early lead
even when training improves other prompts, separating evidence that a
crossover exists from claims about what it means for capability.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: The RLVR-capability debate asks whether reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards teaches a model anything its base could not already do. Since Yue et al. (2025) its central evidence has been a picture: the RL model wins at pass@1, the base wins at pass@256, and the curves cross in between — read as sharpening by one camp ( Yue et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) and contested on metric or horizon by the other ( Wen et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . Where uncertainty is quantified at all, it is per- k k intervals against seed noise ( Zhou, 2026b ; Strozzi, 2026 ) . The missing object is paired inference across sampling budgets: a confidence-band criterion that tests whether an observed crossing is statistically supported and bounds where it occurs. How much can go wrong? Three examples from 1000 paired prompts. Crossings appear in subsamples : a 167-prompt shard of ProRL/base crossed at k = 18 k{=}18 ; the full sample overturned it. Crossings can be insignificant at very large sample sizes : ProRL’s crossing at k = 56 k{=}56 is not statistically established at 1000 × 256 1000{\times}256 generations ( p = .20 p{=}.20 ). And the comparison depends on the per-response token limit : DeepScaleR shows no crossing at 8k, yet at 16k the point estimate changes sign at k = 27 k{=}27 and the dominance test rejects unadjusted ( p = .029 p{=}.029 , not family-wise significant across the five-pair discovery family); the crossing criterion, which requires statistical evidence of a gain and a loss, passes only at 32k (Figure 1 ). The crossover lives at the edge of detectability and moves with measurement choices that routinely go unreported. Figure 1: Four claims, not one: effects of the token limit. DeepScaleR vs. its base, 1000 mixture prompts, three per-response token limits: D ^ ​ ( k ) \hat{D}(k) with 95% pointwise and simultaneous (sup- t t ) bounds L ⁡ ( k ) , U ⁡ ( k ) L(k),U(k) ; the strip colours each k k by the strongest supported claim. A visual sign change appears at 16k, dominance is rejected at 16k and 32k, and a statistically supported sign change (dark-red cell) exists only at 32k; the new-prompt confirmation is in Table 1 . We study the paired difference D ⁡ ( k ) = pass@ ​ k RL − pass@ ​ k base D(k)=\text{pass@}k^{\mathrm{RL}}-\text{pass@}k^{\mathrm{base}} : paired inference tests for crossings (§ 2 ), while a response model explains their shape (§ 4 ). A 32k evaluation on fresh prompts confirms a crossing. Non-detection elsewhere must be read alongside power: under the fitted kernels, dominance-test power is .2 .2 – .6 .6 for the two public pairs (§ 3 ). The main lesson comes after that calibration. Even for a fixed model pair, prompts with the same base success probability p p can have different post-training probabilities q q , and a split-generation test shows these differences repeat beyond sampling noise. So p ↦ q p\mapsto q is not a single curve: we need the distribution of q q among prompts sharing p p , a Markov kernel (§ 5 ). This matters because pass@ k k depends nonlinearly on success probability, so the mean response to training does not determine the whole pass@ k k curve. Contributions. 1. Paired inference and empirical evaluation (§ 2 – 3 ): simultaneous bands for the paired difference curve, a dominance test, and a crossing criterion with a first-loss interval (Proposition 1 ), valid without an operator model. No public pair meets it in the initial evaluations; a 32k-token re-measurement on fresh prompts does, locating the first loss between k = 11 k{=}11 and k = 61 k{=}61 . 2. Power and sample complexity (§ 3 ): simulated from the fitted operators, dominance-test power at realized designs is .01 .01 – .63 .63 ( α = .05 \alpha{=}.05 ); breadth beats depth, and some effects remain hard to detect throughout the tested design grid. 3. The operator is a kernel, not a function (§ 5 ): a split-generation residual test rejects the deterministic map p ↦ q p\mapsto q on all thirteen pairs and two non-Qwen bases; the operator is a Markov kernel H ⁡ ( q ∣ p ) H(q\mid p) whose nonparametric refit predicts crossings in independent generations for the same prompts and improves power estimation. 4. Tail theorem and controlled diagnostics (§ 4 , § 6 ): any operator with tail elasticity β tail > 1 \beta_{\mathrm{tail}}>1 must invert if it is ever ahead (Theorem 2 ), extending to kernels under a power-law support condition; a crossover alone cannot separate sharpening from genuine gain, and controlled runs separate GRPO from SFT in fitted slope and curve shape.

On the event that the band covers D D : (i) if there exist j < ℓ j<\ell with L ⁡ ( j ) > 0 L(j)>0 and U ⁡ ( ℓ ) < 0 U(\ell)<0 , then D D has a positive-to-negative sign change in [ j , ℓ ] [j,\ell] ; (ii) the first-loss budget κ = inf { k : D ⁡ ( k ) < 0 } \kappa=\inf\{k:D(k)<0\} (the first sampling budget k k at which the trained model is worse; it equals the first positive-to-negative crossing only when an earlier region with a positive lower confidence bound exists) satisfies κ ∈ [ κ ¯ , κ ¯ ] \kappa\in[\underline{\kappa},\overline{\kappa}] with κ ¯ = 1 + max ⁡ { j ≥ 0 : L ⁡ ( r ) > 0 ​ ∀ r ≤ j } \underline{\kappa}=1+\max\{j\geq 0:L(r)>0\ \forall r\leq j\} (the constraint is vacuous at j = 0 j=0 , so κ ¯ = 1 \underline{\kappa}=1 whenever L ⁡ ( 1 ) ≤ 0 L(1)\leq 0 ) and κ ¯ = min ⁡ { j : U ⁡ ( j ) < 0 } \overline{\kappa}=\min\{j:U(j)<0\} ( = ∞ =\infty if the upper bound is never negative). sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We generate paired samples for two public RLVR pairs sharing the base R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview and ProRL ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . Prompts: 500 MATH-500 + + 500 DeepScaleR-corpus (pooled 50/50; source-equality rejects, so claims are mixture-specific). Decoding: temperature .6 .6 , top- p p .95 .95 ; symbolic-equivalence verification; ≈ 350 \approx 350 A30-GPU-hours. Every result reports its protocol. Our verifiers require full worked solutions, so the guessing floor of Dragoi et al. (2025) — which truncates polynomial tails and manufactures a crossover near its reciprocal — is negligible at k ≤ 256 k\leq 256 (Appendix D ).

sections.heading: Finding 1: a visible crossing need not be statistically supported.
sections.text: ProRL’s crossing at k = 56 k{=}56 is not statistically established ( p = .20 p{=}.20 ). DeepScaleR at 16k is the strongest initial discovery ( p = .029 p{=}.029 ), but the crossing criterion is not met, it is not family-wise significant under Holm over the five-pair discovery family, and a fresh-prompt check at the same token limit does not reproduce the crossing evidence ( p = .91 p{=}.91 ); no public pair yields a family-wise significant dominance violation at the discovery stage. The pre-specified 32k new-prompt run tests whether the crossing carries.

sections.heading: Finding 2: the crossing is confirmed on fresh prompts at 32k.
sections.text: The analysis plan was specified before sampling (Appendix G ): re-measurement of DeepScaleR at 32 32 k tokens, n = n ′ = 128 n{=}n^{\prime}{=}128 , on 1060 1060 deduplicated problems from OlympiadBench, Gaokao-2023-EN, AMC23, and AIME24; primary endpoint the crossing criterion at k ≤ 128 k\leq 128 . The fresh run passes: L ⁡ ( k ) > 0 L(k)>0 for k ≤ 10 k\leq 10 , U ⁡ ( k ) < 0 U(k)<0 for k ≥ 61 k\geq 61 , giving κ ∈ [ 11 , 61 ] \kappa\in[11,61] (dominance p = .0027 p{=}.0027 ; pre-registered on the frozen sparse grid as κ ∈ [ 9 , 64 ] \kappa\in[9,64] , with the dense-grid restatement in Appendix G ). The band’s late-loss margin ( δ − = | U ⁡ ( 128 ) | = 3.7 × 10 − 3 \delta_{-}{=}|U(128)|{=}3.7\times 10^{-3} ) is an order of magnitude below the early gain ( δ + = L ⁡ ( 1 ) = .0655 \delta_{+}{=}L(1){=}.0655 ): the reversal is statistically visible, but small. The point estimates are a 7.6 7.6 percentage-point gain at k = 1 k=1 and a 2.0 2.0 -point loss at k = 128 k=128 . Base and RL truncation rates remain 7.8 % 7.8\% and 0.7 % 0.7\% . In a sensitivity analysis that repairs each failed base truncation with probability .25 .25 , the simultaneous band still supports a crossing. This is a specified repair scenario, not an observation of continued decoding; the zero-truncation subset retains an early gain but no supported late loss (Appendix G ).

sections.heading: Finding 3: domain and protocol sensitivity.
sections.text: On HumanEval+/MBPP+ ( n = 64 n{=}64 , execution-verified), neither pair meets the crossing criterion ( p = .38 p{=}.38 , .55 .55 ), while the fitted logit slopes (§ 4 ) nearly match their math values (Appendix A.3 ): the slope is stable across domains but statistical evidence of a crossing is not. At a 2048-token limit both models are worse than base at every k k ( p < .001 p<.001 ); at 8192 both improve at pass@1 and nothing is significant — one unreported protocol choice flips both sign and significance.

sections.heading: How much power does the dominance test have?
sections.text: The power analysis developed in § 5 simulates fitted kernels, including the controlled runs of § 6 ( G G : rollout group size). It quantifies dominance-test power, not power to detect a crossing: low power to detect a loss cautions against reading failure to detect a crossing as no crossing. At the realized design, power is .63 .63 for DeepScaleR-16k and .21 .21 for ProRL-16k (Table 15 , Appendix H ). Breadth beats depth : DeepScaleR-16k reaches .877 .877 at m = 4000 m{=}4000 , n = 128 n{=}128 but only .489 .489 at equal cost with m = 1000 m{=}1000 , n = 512 n{=}512 (both at the Holm threshold α = .01 \alpha{=}.01 ; the first design gives .967 .967 at α = .05 \alpha{=}.05 ), because the between-prompt term does not shrink with n n . More sampling may still be insufficient : the G = 4 G{=}4 arm never reaches .80 .80 on the tested ( m , n ) (m,n) grid; even a 3.3 × 10 7 3.3\times 10^{7} -generation design gives .060 .060 . These finite-grid results do not establish impossibility with unlimited total generations.

sections.heading: 4 A simple response model and its limits
sections.text: A single curve from base success p p to post-training success q q describes who gains and loses, and connects changes on the hardest prompts ( p p near zero) to large- k k behavior. Testing its limits motivates the conditional distribution of § 5 ; the paired inference above does not depend on it.

sections.text: In GRPO with rollout group size G G , an all-failure group receives zero policy-gradient advantage — probability ( 1 − p ) G (1-p)^{G} per step. This is already a restricted kernel: at fixed p p , q q is either zero or T β , γ ​ ( p ) T_{\beta,\gamma}(p) . The nonzero response is still a single curve; § 5 tests for dispersion beyond this atom. The ( 1 − p ) G (1-p)^{G} form is specific to group-relative advantage estimation, where an all-failure group of size G G yields identically zero advantages for every member; methods with a learned or leave-one-out baseline do not share this exact hazard. The fitted π ^ 0 \hat{\pi}_{0} does not separate the two objective families — SimpleRL-Zoo, group-relative, fits .00 .00 (Table 3 ) — so we read it as an excess-zero index under a stated G G , not as a measurement of a support-collapse mechanism. Theorem 2 (Tail exponent and asymptotic crossover) . Suppose F F has density f ⁡ ( p ) ∼ c ​ p a − 1 f(p)\sim c\,p^{a-1} as p → 0 + p\to 0^{+} , π 0 = 0 \pi_{0}=0 , and the operator is regularly varying at the hard tail : T ⁡ ( p ) ∼ C ​ p β tail T(p)\sim C\,p^{\beta_{\mathrm{tail}}} as p → 0 + p\to 0^{+} for some C > 0 C>0 , and T T is bounded away from zero on compact subsets of ( 0 , 1 ] (0,1] (equivalently inf p ∈ [ δ , 1 ] T ⁡ ( p ) > 0 \inf_{p\in[\delta,1]}T(p)>0 for every δ > 0 \delta>0 ; automatic for the affine-logit link, and needed only to make the non-tail segment geometrically negligible) — the affine-logit link equation 1 is the special case β tail = β \beta_{\mathrm{tail}}=\beta , C = e γ C=e^{\gamma} , but no global link assumption is needed. Consequently, if β tail > 1 \beta_{\mathrm{tail}}>1 then D ⁡ ( k ) < 0 D(k)<0 for all sufficiently large k k ; if in addition D ⁡ ( k 0 ) > 0 D(k_{0})>0 at some finite k 0 k_{0} , the curves have at least one positive-to-negative crossing. In the regime p ⋆ → 0 p^{\star}\to 0 the crossing scale under the affine link is log ⁡ k ⋆ = log ⁡ 1 − p ⋆ p ⋆ + O ⁡ ( 1 ) \log k^{\star}=\log\frac{1-p^{\star}}{p^{\star}}+O(1) (closed form in Appendix A ). If instead π 0 > 0 \pi_{0}>0 , then G 1 ​ ( k ) → π 0 ​ 𝔼 ​ ( 1 − p ) G > 0 G_{1}(k)\to\pi_{0}\,\mathbb{E}(1-p)^{G}>0 while G 0 ​ ( k ) → 0 G_{0}(k)\to 0 , giving a second crossover scale k 0 ⋆ k^{\star}_{0} ; which mechanism binds is an empirical finding. Theorem 3 (Single crossing) . Let π 0 = 0 \pi_{0}=0 . If T T has one interior fixed point, preserves its two sides, and crosses the diagonal in one direction, then D ⁡ ( k ) D(k) changes sign at most once: positive to negative when T T crosses from below, and negative to positive when it crosses from above. Together with Theorem 2 , an early gain and β tail > 1 \beta_{\mathrm{tail}}>1 imply a unique inversion. The precise conditions and proof are in Appendix B.3 . Thus two statistically supported sign changes falsify this class of single-fixed-point, side-preserving operators. Under these tail assumptions, β tail > 1 \beta_{\mathrm{tail}}>1 means the hardest prompts retain a vanishing fraction of base success ( T ⁡ ( p ) / p → 0 T(p)/p\to 0 ), eventually overturning any early lead — asymptotic reversal, not every finite- k k crossing. Gains on other prompts can coexist with such losses, so the crossovers of Yue et al. (2025) do not rule out substantial gain; conversely a pure positive shift ( β tail = 1 \beta_{\mathrm{tail}}=1 , SimpleRL-Zoo in Finding 4) improves prompts without crossing (Appendix B ).

sections.heading: What a fitted slope summarizes.
sections.text: When h i h_{i} varies, the population logit projection β proj = 1 / τ + Cov ⁡ ( h i , logit ⁡ p i ) / Var ⁡ ( logit ⁡ p i ) \beta_{\mathrm{proj}}=1/\tau+\mathrm{Cov}(h_{i},\operatorname{logit}p_{i})/\mathrm{Var}(\operatorname{logit}p_{i}) need not equal the tail exponent β tail \beta_{\mathrm{tail}} , and under misspecification EM targets the KL projection of the joint count law onto the working family. Both depend on the prompt population and evaluation settings; neither is automatically the hardest-prompt asymptotic slope.

sections.heading: Estimation and checks.
sections.text: Grid EM jointly fits the base mixing law and response parameters ( L = 200 L{=}200 ; Appendix C ), avoiding the attenuation of a plug-in fit (ProRL: β ^ = .88 \hat{\beta}=.88 versus 1.58 1.58 ). The pre-specified checks test the base-curve fit, affine link, and zero-atom stability (M1–M3; Appendix D ). The affine link is rejected ( p = .005 p=.005 ); a monotone spline gives tail-slope estimates stable across knots on deep-sampled pairs but unidentified at n = 64 n=64 . These remain deterministic-link summaries: allowing conditional dispersion changes their interpretation (§ 5 ).

sections.heading: Finding 4: fitted slopes vary across pairs and evaluation settings.
sections.text: β ^ proj \hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{proj}} spans from a pure location shift (SimpleRL-Zoo: 1.00 1.00 [ 0.96 , 1.05 ] [0.96,1.05] , the only non-rejection of the affine link) to sharpening (DeepScaleR 1.26 1.26 [ 1.20 , 1.33 ] [1.20,1.33] , ProRL 1.58 1.58 [ 1.40 , 1.77 ] [1.40,1.77] ; CIs excluding 1 1 ); LUFFY and ORZ are off-policy or token-limit-confounded and excluded from recipe-level statements (Table 3 , Appendix A ). Each value is a projection of the pair’s joint law under a stated protocol, not a physical constant of the training recipe: on DeepScaleR it replicates on fresh prompts ( 1.41 1.41 at 16k, 1.31 1.31 on the 32k fresh population) while the crossing evidence at 16k does not.

sections.heading: Why test for missing variation?
sections.text: For ProRL-16k the working model predicts dominance-test power .98 .98 , yet the observed p = .20 p{=}.20 is non-significant (Appendix C ). That alone does not refute it, but together with the rejected link and the variation in h i h_{i} it motivates the next section’s direct test for reproducible variation at fixed p p .

sections.heading: Why base success is not enough.
sections.text: Fix the base and trained checkpoints. A kernel H ⁡ ( q ∣ p ) H(q\mid p) describes variation across prompts with the same base success p p , not variation across training seeds or the randomness of individual answers. Its mean T ⁡ ( p ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ Q ∣ P = p ] T(p)=\mathbb{E}[Q\mid P=p] summarizes the average response, but for k > 1 k>1 the conditional pass@ k k is 1 − 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( 1 − Q ) k ∣ P = p ] 1-\mathbb{E}[(1-Q)^{k}\mid P=p] , generally not 1 − ( 1 − T ⁡ ( p ) ) k 1-(1-T(p))^{k} . Two prompt populations can therefore share a mean response and have different pass@ k k curves. Figure 2 tests whether this missing variation is real and useful for prediction. For example, at fixed p p , compare Q = .5 Q=.5 for every prompt with an equal mixture of Q = .1 Q=.1 and .9 .9 . Both have pass@1 of .5 .5 , but pass@2 is .75 .75 versus .59 .59 : using only the mean success probability overestimates the gain from repeated attempts on the same prompt. Equation 2 suggests one possible source: h i h_{i} depends on how probability is distributed within correct and incorrect solutions, information not specified by p p alone. ProRL prompts with no successes in repeated sampling illustrate one failure pattern: their modal-answer share is .88 .88 , with the base’s modal error inherited in half the cases (Appendix D ). This does not make answer concentration a general predictor of RL gains or losses; the test below concerns the dispersion itself. Figure 2: The operator is a kernel, not a function (ProRL-16k, 1000 1000 prompts, n = n ′ = 256 n{=}n^{\prime}{=}256 ). (a) ( p ^ i , q ^ i ) (\hat{p}_{i},\hat{q}_{i}) against the best deterministic mean link; 40% of prompts fall outside its 95% binomial envelope (5% expected). (b) Residuals from two disjoint generation halves (cross-fitted mean removed); binomial noise is independent across halves, so the diagonal ( ρ = .93 \rho{=}.93 ) is replicable heterogeneity. (c) The kernel fitted on generation half A A predicts half B B on the same prompts and vice versa: predicted crossing 67 67 vs. 62 62 held out; the inset magnifies the point crossings, not statistical evidence of a crossing.

sections.heading: The split-generation test.
sections.text: Split each prompt’s post-RL generations into disjoint halves A / B A/B and its base generations likewise; remove a cross-fitted mean; check whether the halves’ residuals covary across prompts. Mean-link error can mimic dispersion, so bootstrap calibration reruns the pipeline under two fitted nulls: a deterministic spline and a spline plus zero atom. The latter tests dispersion beyond the atom. A base-only negative control gives | z | < 2 |z|<2 (Appendix E ). All thirteen pairs reject both nulls ( p < .002 p<.002 ; Table 5 ). The replicable dispersion is large (RMS sd .10 .10 – .15 .15 for DeepScaleR, ProRL, and every controlled run, against ≈ .03 \approx.03 from binomial noise) and patterned: SimpleRL-Zoo is smallest ( .04 .04 ); in-domain ProRL carries 2.2 × 2.2\times the dispersion of transfer DeepScaleR. Fixing base difficulty does not fix what RLVR does to a prompt; the operator is a Markov kernel H ⁡ ( q ∣ p ) H(q\mid p) , and T ⁡ ( p ) T(p) is only its mean.

sections.heading: The kernel refit.
sections.text: We re-estimate the joint mixing law of ( P , Q ) (P,Q) by a 2D NPMLE (Appendix E.2 ). Three consequences. First , part of fitted zero-inflation was continuous dispersion in disguise: a beta-binomial conditional cuts π ^ 0 \hat{\pi}_{0} from .08 .08 to .03 .03 (DeepScaleR) and .23 .23 to .12 .12 (ProRL); the surviving component belongs to the pair whose zeros resist prefix rescue (§ 6 ). Second , it changes the power assessment of § 4 : ProRL’s affine-predicted power .98 .98 becomes .21 .21 (Table 15 ), making non-rejection the modal outcome. Third , generation-split validation fits the kernel on one disjoint half and predicts the other: predictions match crossings in independent generations on the same prompts (DeepScaleR 29 29 vs 28 28 ; ProRL 67 67 vs 62 62 ; four no-crossing verdicts reproduced), and held-out likelihood prefers the kernel by ≈ 10 3 \approx 10^{3} units where dispersion is large relative to deterministic fits (Appendices E.3 , E.2 ). A beta-binomial conditional is better on per-prompt held-out likelihood, whereas the nonparametric kernel predicts the two cross-fitted crossing locations more closely (errors 1 / 5 1/5 versus 5 / 13 5/13 draws). The advantage therefore depends on the prediction target; both support conditional dispersion.

sections.heading: Replication on non-Qwen bases.
sections.text: The same split test on Llama-3.1-8B and DeepSeek-Math-7B (SimpleRL-Zoo recipe, n = n ′ = 128 n{=}n^{\prime}{=}128 ) rejects determinism in both ( z = 12.2 z{=}12.2 , 7.1 7.1 ; p ≤ .0025 p\leq.0025 ; placebo null), and the kernel again dominates the spline in likelihood. The dispersion is therefore not a Qwen-family artifact; neither pair meets the crossing criterion (Appendix E.4 ).

sections.heading: What drives the late- k k loss under a kernel.
sections.text: Theorem 2 and Remark 1 give a sufficient deterministic route to inversion — the hardest prompts retaining a vanishing fraction of base success — but the fitted kernels do not take it: their conditional-mean slope falls below one on every pair once a dispersion family is fitted ( 1.26 → .88 1.26\to.88 , 1.58 → .72 1.58\to.72 , 2.08 → .58 2.08\to.58 ; Table 6 ), and collapsing each kernel onto its own conditional mean removes every crossing inside the observation window (Table 2 ). This comparison holds both the base success distribution and 𝔼 ⁡ [ Q ∣ P ] \mathbb{E}[Q\mid P] fixed, changing only conditional dispersion. The measured crossings are instead dispersion-driven: q ↦ ( 1 − q ) k q\mapsto(1-q)^{k} is strictly convex for k ≥ 2 k\geq 2 , so spread at fixed p p inflates post-RL failure above the mean link’s prediction, and what supplies it is a minority of prompts locked near q ≈ 0 q\approx 0 at difficulties where the mean still improves. Consequently β ^ proj > 1 \hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{proj}}>1 and the spline β ^ tail > 1 \hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{tail}}>1 are not measurements of tail elasticity under a kernel, and Theorem 2 remains a statement about which operators must invert rather than a description of the mechanism behind the inversions measured here. First positive-to-nonpositive crossings of fitted curves; “none” means none through k = 2 × 10 5 k=2\times 10^{5} . These model comparisons are not statistical confirmation of population crossings. Full details are in Appendix E.2 . Remark 1 (What survives under a kernel) . Within-window claims (dominance tests, crossing criteria, κ \kappa -intervals) never used an operator and are untouched. Theorem 2 extends: if H ( ⋅ ∣ p ) H(\cdot\mid p) is supported on [ c 1 ​ p β , c 2 ​ p β ] [c_{1}p^{\beta},\,c_{2}p^{\beta}] as p → 0 p\to 0 , monotonicity of q ↦ ( 1 − q ) k q\mapsto(1-q)^{k} sandwiches G 1 ​ ( k ) G_{1}(k) between two deterministic curves, so the failure exponent is still a / β a/\beta and a β > 1 \beta>1 kernel that is ever ahead must invert (Appendix B ). Neither condition holds for the fitted kernels: their conditional-mean slope is below one, and the mass locked near q ≈ 0 q\approx 0 pushes the lower support below any c 1 ​ p β c_{1}p^{\beta} , so the measured inversions come from that lower tail instead (paragraph above; Appendix E.2 ). Theorem 3 does not transfer: uniqueness used a single fixed point of T T , which a kernel need not have, and the crossing criterion never relied on it. β ^ proj \hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{proj}} remains a summary under the specified evaluation settings; extrapolation beyond the measured range depends on the lower tail of H ( ⋅ ∣ p ) H(\cdot\mid p) .

sections.heading: Finding 5: GRPO has a greater average logit slope than SFT.
sections.text: From a single base (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B; 8k MATH problems) we train GRPO at G ∈ { 4 , 8 , 16 } G\in\{4,8,16\} (KL 10 − 3 10^{-3} ) and SFT on reference solutions ( n = 128 n{=}128 , n ′ = 64 n^{\prime}{=}64 ; 3072 tokens). GRPO gives β ^ proj = 1.67 \hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{proj}}=1.67 [ 1.54 , 1.82 ] [1.54,1.82] ( G = 4 G{=}4 ), 1.76 1.76 [ 1.61 , 1.92 ] [1.61,1.92] ( G = 16 G{=}16 ), versus SFT’s .93 .93 [ .85 , 1.03 ] [.85,1.03] ; deepening to n = 256 n{=}256 barely moves the contrasts (Appendix D ). A flexible-link analysis (curves, local slopes and contrasts in Figure 5 , Appendix D ) averages the local logit slope uniformly between the 20th and 80th percentiles of base logit difficulty (the average logit slope or integrated elasticity, distinct from β proj \beta_{\mathrm{proj}} and β tail \beta_{\mathrm{tail}} ). It preserves the GRPO > {>} SFT ordering but places SFT above one as well ( 1.88 1.88 , 1.99 1.99 , 1.39 1.39 ): “opposite sides of a pure shift” is an affine artefact, and the contrast band supports an integrated ordering, not pointwise dominance. Averaging only over p ∈ [ .027 , .554 ] p\in[.027,.554] , it also carries no implication of an inversion: SFT stays positive through k = 256 k{=}256 ( D ⁡ ( 256 ) = + .009 D(256)=+.009 , Appendix D ) at 1.39 1.39 .

sections.heading: Group size, power, and prompts with no observed successes.
sections.text: G G barely moves the fitted slope ( 1.67 1.67 , 1.68 1.68 , 1.76 1.76 at G = 4 , 8 , 16 G{=}4,8,16 ). All three GRPO arms have point-estimate crossings, but none is statistically supported ( p ≥ .20 p\geq.20 ); detectability depends on the arm and sampling design (Table 15 ). All controlled-run prompts with no observed successes yield correct answers under unrestricted decoding; some ProRL prompts still yield none (Appendices D , F ).

sections.heading: Horizon.
sections.text: These arms run 100 GRPO updates, one to two orders of magnitude short of the public checkpoints with confirmed crossings ( ∼ \sim 1,750 steps for DeepScaleR, ∼ \sim 3,000 for ProRL), and zero-atom severity tracks that horizon ( π ^ 0 \hat{\pi}_{0} across the three: controlled 0 0 , DeepScaleR .08 .08 , ProRL .23 .23 ; Appendix D ). They therefore bound what a short horizon does to the operator rather than reproducing the regime in which the crossings of § 3 appear, so their non-detections should be read jointly with the power figures of Table 15 .

sections.heading: The RLVR-capability debate.
sections.text: Yue et al. (2025) established the crossover across six RLVR algorithms and read it as evidence that RLVR does not exceed the base; Wen et al. (2026) credit intermediate reasoning (CoT-Pass@K); Wu et al. (2025) characterize RLVR as support-constrained conservative reweighting, the mechanism closest to ours; Liu et al. (2025) argue prolonged training expands the boundary. Zhou (2026b) and Strozzi (2026) attach seed-level intervals to crossovers; Kim et al. (2025) bin post-RL gains by base success rate, the descriptive precursor of our fitted map. All treat the effect as a deterministic map on prompt-level success rates ( Fan et al., 2026 , also) , the assumption § 5 rejects. Clay et al. (2026) manipulate base probabilities, rewards, and training prompts in controlled tasks, showing that dense rewards can overcome sparse-reward failures for behaviors with low initial probability. These interventions complement our paired inference: a crossover alone does not identify a learning mechanism, and low initial probability is not absence from the base distribution.

sections.heading: Statistical treatments of pass@ k k .
sections.text: Kazdan et al. (2025) extrapolate pass@ k k within one model by beta-binomial fit; we adopt their estimator as our base stage. Levi (2026) is the closest theory: in a solvable supervised model the pass@ k k exponent rises with data, where our mechanism predicts reward-driven redistribution that flattens it ( a ↦ a / β tail a\mapsto a/\beta_{\mathrm{tail}} ); Finding 5 tests the within-support direction. Repeated-sampling scaling originates with Brown et al. (2024) , its power laws derived from difficulty heterogeneity by Schaeffer et al. (2025) . Hariri et al. (2026) replace pass@ k k with a single-model posterior and Dragoi et al. (2025) show pass@ k → 1 k\to 1 by guessing; Miller (2024) ; Bowyer et al. (2025) treat error bars for scalar accuracy, Bay & Yearick (2026) model the within-prompt correlation our bootstrap exploits, and Zhou (2026a) propose four tail-exponent checks that we adopt. Hazard-curve crossing procedures exist ( Cheng et al., 2009 ) but assume independent arms.

sections.heading: Exponential tilting.
sections.text: Huang et al. (2024) characterize KL-regularized RL as an exponential tilt, and GX-Chen et al. (2025) , Mroueh (2025) , Polson et al. (2026) and Tomihari & Sato (2026) give variational, Bayesian, and distillation views of the same structure. All characterize the optimal policy form; we take the tilt as given and study the paired comparison and its statistical structure.

sections.heading: 8 Discussion
sections.text: A visible crossover need not be statistically established, and failure to detect one need not mean absence; paired bands and power analysis separate these claims. The kernel result explains why base success alone is insufficient: prompts at the same p p respond differently to training, so a fitted slope summarizes but does not replace that distribution, and extrapolation beyond the measured range requires checking H ⁡ ( q ∣ p ) H(q\mid p) .

sections.heading: A reporting protocol.
sections.text: Four recommendations follow. 1. Check truncation and token-limit sensitivity. Report truncation on both sides and whether raising the limit changes the comparison; distinguish observed outcomes from hypothetical repairs. 2. Consider more prompts before deeper sampling. Choose n n to cover the target sampling budgets k ≤ n k\leq n , then assess the power gained by spending on more prompts. Pooling benchmarks changes the target population (Appendix H ). 3. Use simultaneous bands when searching across k k . A crossing requires a gain at smaller k k and a loss at larger k k (Proposition 1 ); rejecting dominance alone does not establish it, though pointwise intervals remain appropriate at a single pre-specified k k . 4. Run the split-generation check before quoting an exponent. It needs no extra sampling, and replicable residual covariance means a fitted slope summarizes a distribution of responses, not a single curve.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: The crossing is confirmed on fresh prompts, but its late-loss margin at 32k is small. Kernel validation holds out generations, not prompts; the non-Qwen and scale checks support the dispersion diagnostic without replicating effect sizes, and the single two-scale comparison confounds parameter count with math-specialized pretraining. Beyond-window quantities ( k ⋆ k^{\star} , confidence sets) are fitted-law extrapolations, so safety readings at large k k are questions the framework can pose, not conclusions established here. Domain evidence is narrow (Appendix D ).

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: This work analyzes publicly released model checkpoints on public benchmark problems and introduces no new data collection involving human subjects. Improved statistical rigor for pass@ k k claims bears on safety evaluation, where overconfident “safe at k = 1 k=1 ” claims can mask large- k k risk.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: All sampling configurations (decoding parameters, per-response token limits, verifier), per-prompt counts, per-generation correctness bits (used by the split-generation test), fitted objects, and the estimation/inference/heterogeneity code ( passk-inference ) accompany the submission as an anonymized supplementary archive, together with the pre-specified model checks M1–M3, the tail-exponent checks, and the decision rules and realized outcomes of Appendix G . A public repository link will be provided at camera-ready.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: Large language models were used as coding and writing assistants throughout this project: drafting and refactoring analysis code, managing compute jobs, literature search, and prose editing, all under author direction and review. The theoretical results, experimental design, and interpretation were verified by the authors; all numerical claims trace to released code and per-prompt counts.

sections.heading: Appendix A Working-model supplement
sections.text: This appendix collects the results that live entirely inside the affine working model of § 4 : the identifiability theorem, the closed-form crossover scale, the Fieller set for k ⋆ k^{\star} , and the public-pair projections. § 5 shows the deterministic operator is misspecified, so every quantity here is a fitted summary under specified evaluation settings rather than a property of a training recipe.

sections.heading: A.1 Identifiability
sections.text: Theorem 4 (Identifiability) . The set is 𝒞 1 − α = { κ : 2 [ ℓ ( η ^ ) − sup η : κ full ​ ( η ) = κ ℓ ( η ) ] ≤ χ 1 , 1 − α 2 } \mathcal{C}_{1-\alpha}=\{\kappa:\ 2[\ell(\hat{\eta})-\sup_{\eta:\kappa_{\mathrm{full}}(\eta)=\kappa}\ell(\eta)]\leq\chi^{2}_{1,1-\alpha}\} . The constrained supremum is computed with π 0 \pi_{0} (and a , b , β a,b,\beta ) in the outer profile and γ \gamma as the inner root of κ full ​ ( η ) = κ \kappa_{\mathrm{full}}(\eta)=\kappa . Two properties of the inner problem matter. On the π 0 = 0 \pi_{0}=0 slice, κ full \kappa_{\mathrm{full}} is strictly increasing in γ \gamma and the root is unique. For π 0 > 0 \pi_{0}>0 it is nondecreasing but bounded above : as γ → ∞ \gamma\to\infty the continuous part of G 1 G_{1} vanishes and the crossing saturates at the atom-driven scale k 0 ⋆ ​ ( a , b , π 0 , G ) k^{\star}_{0}(a,b,\pi_{0},G) , which does not depend on γ \gamma (numerically, e.g. F = Beta ⁡ ( .6 , 2 ) F=\mathrm{Beta}(.6,2) , G = 8 G{=}8 , β = 1.2 \beta{=}1.2 , π 0 = .1 \pi_{0}{=}.1 : κ full \kappa_{\mathrm{full}} rises 8 → 461 8\to 461 over γ ∈ [ 0.5 , 8 ] \gamma\in[0.5,8] and is constant thereafter). Slices of ( a , b , β , π 0 ) (a,b,\beta,\pi_{0}) with sup γ κ full < κ \sup_{\gamma}\kappa_{\mathrm{full}}<\kappa therefore admit no root; they are infeasible for that κ \kappa and are excluded from the constrained supremum — the implementation returns − ∞ -\infty for them, so the outer profile moves π 0 \pi_{0} (and β \beta ) to a feasible slice when one exists. This is what makes the large- κ \kappa limit of the constrained fit chase the joint corner { β → 1 , π 0 → 0 } \{\beta\to 1,\pi_{0}\to 0\} rather than any single parameter. κ full \kappa_{\mathrm{full}} must not be conflated with the continuous-branch crossing k cont ⋆ k^{\star}_{\mathrm{cont}} of Theorem 2 , which is defined under π 0 = 0 \pi_{0}=0 and has the ( β − 1 ) − 1 (\beta-1)^{-1} Fieller singularity: as β ↓ 1 \beta\downarrow 1 with γ > 0 \gamma>0 , k cont ⋆ → ∞ k^{\star}_{\mathrm{cont}}\to\infty . For κ full \kappa_{\mathrm{full}} that implication holds only on the π 0 = 0 \pi_{0}=0 slice : when π 0 > 0 \pi_{0}>0 the post-RL failure curve converges to the positive floor π 0 ​ 𝔼 ​ ( 1 − p ) G \pi_{0}\,\mathbb{E}(1-p)^{G} while the base curve vanishes, so a finite atom-driven crossing exists even at β = 1 \beta=1 . Consequently the unboundedness of the reported set is not decided by whether β = 1 \beta=1 can be rejected; it is decided by whether the profiled likelihood can exclude the joint boundary { β → 1 , π 0 → 0 } \{\beta\to 1,\ \pi_{0}\to 0\} — the constrained fit at large κ \kappa chases exactly that corner, and the set contains a neighbourhood of + ∞ +\infty only if the corner is within the likelihood-ratio threshold. This is the honest report ( Fieller, 1954 ) : “no sharpening and no floor” jointly not excluded. sections.heading: Rejected alternative.
sections.text: The truncated-likelihood two-part estimator (link fit on d > 0 d>0 under the zero-truncated binomial; π 0 \pi_{0} from excess zeros) is upward-biased everywhere in the same design — π ^ 0 ∈ [ .30 , .45 ] \hat{\pi}_{0}\in[.30,.45] at true π 0 = 0 \pi_{0}=0 — because plug-in difficulty estimates plus link flexibility overstate q q at low p p and misclassify continuous zeros as a latent atom. We document it as a negative result.

sections.heading: Extended validation (E0).
sections.text: Full simulation details for the results summarized in § 4 . 400 replicates per cell, α = .05 \alpha=.05 . The dominance test is nominal at the all-binding null (rejection .050 .050 – .058 .058 across m ∈ [ 250 , 8000 ] m\in[250,8000] ), exactly conservative in the interior of H 0 H_{0} (zero rejections under a pure shift and under β > 1 \beta>1 with k ⋆ > K k^{\star}>K ), and powerful where it should be (deep crossing: power 1.0 1.0 from m = 250 m=250 ). The comparison with reality is informative: the fitted ProRL-16k model implies power .98 .98 at m = 1000 m=1000 while the real data do not reject ( p = .20 p=.20 ), independently confirming that the affine fit overstates tail redistribution, echoing the M2 rejection. Appendix E.3 resolves the anomaly: under the kernel refit the implied power is .22 .22 ( 300 300 replicates; .207 .207 on the 1000 1000 -replicate design grid of Table 16 ) and the observed non-rejection is the modal outcome.

sections.heading: Baseline comparison.
sections.text: Against the natural alternative — Bonferroni/Holm min- p p over pointwise one-sided tests on the same k k -grid — the multiplier test at m = 1000 m{=}1000 , n = n ′ = 256 n{=}n^{\prime}{=}256 holds size where Bonferroni is conservative ( .052 .052 vs. .015 .015 at the all-binding null with realistic across- k k correlation) and converts that into power exactly where it matters: .215 .215 vs. .110 .110 against the kernel-fitted shallow alternative (ProRL-16k), .985 .985 vs. .950 .950 against the deep affine alternative (400 replicates). Exploiting the across- k k correlation roughly doubles power against the effect sizes actually in dispute. For the Fieller set we compared three constructions. The delta interval fails exactly as predicted: at true β = 1 \beta=1 it never covers ( 0 % 0\% across m m ; a bounded interval cannot contain k ⋆ = ∞ k^{\star}=\infty ). A Wald-form Fieller quadratic goes correctly unbounded at β = 1 \beta=1 but undercovers systematically (53–85% at β = 1 \beta=1 ; its unboundedness event is a badly-sized Wald test of β = 1 \beta=1 ). The reported construction is profile-likelihood-ratio inversion, with unboundedness decided by the κ → ∞ \kappa\to\infty limit of the constrained fit — the β = 1 \beta=1 boundary model. Coverage: .93 .93 – .97 .97 across all cells ( β ∈ { 1.0 , 1.05 , 1.1 , 1.2 , 1.4 } × m ∈ { 500 , 2000 } \beta\in\{1.0,1.05,1.1,1.2,1.4\}\times m\in\{500,2000\} , 300 replicates each), including .947 .947 at the boundary β = 1 \beta=1 , m = 2000 m=2000 where the delta method covers 0 % 0\% and the Wald form 53 % 53\% . The truncated-likelihood shortcut for separating a latent atom from link curvature (fit the link on d > 0 d>0 , read π 0 \pi_{0} off excess zeros) is rejected by simulation — biased upward even at true π 0 = 0 \pi_{0}=0 — whereas the joint EM recovers π 0 \pi_{0} within ± .01 \pm.01 under both affine and kinked true links at every n ′ ∈ { 8 , 64 , 256 } n^{\prime}\in\{8,64,256\} .

sections.heading: Appendix D Experimental details
sections.text: Figure 3: The inference machinery, checked against its own claims. Left: size of the dominance test (2,000 replicates, m = 400 m{=}400 , K = 6 K{=}6 , B = 999 B{=}999 ; bars are ± 1.96 \pm 1.96 Monte Carlo standard errors). The top four cells vary the null mean : the test is nominal at the all-binding boundary and conservative everywhere inside H 0 H_{0} , confirming that D ≡ 0 D\equiv 0 is the worst case among mean drifts. The bottom three fix D ≡ 0 D\equiv 0 and vary only the nuisance correlation ; all three sit at nominal, which no procedure calibrated to a single “ D ≡ 0 D\equiv 0 law” could achieve — the prompt-level multiplier bootstrap re-estimates the covariance from the data at hand. Middle: level and power against the number of prompts; the configuration fitted to ProRL-16k needs m ≈ 1000 m\approx 1000 for power near one, while a genuinely shallow crossing is never detected at these sample sizes. A separate seven-cell study checks Theorem 1 exactly as stated ( 𝒯 m = min k ⁡ D ^ ​ ( k ) / σ ^ ​ ( k ) \mathcal{T}_{m}=\min_{k}\hat{D}(k)/\hat{\sigma}(k) against the multiplier quantile q ^ α \hat{q}_{\alpha} , no extra m \sqrt{m} ; 2000 replicates, m = 400 m=400 , K = 6 K=6 , B = 999 B=999 , α = .05 \alpha=.05 ; Monte Carlo standard error ≈ .005 \approx.005 ). sections.heading: Sampling.
sections.text: vLLM, temperature .6 .6 , top- p p .95 .95 ; one shared seed family per token limit; prompts formatted with each model’s chat template plus a boxed-answer instruction; scoring by symbolic equivalence (math-verify) with a 5s timeout per generation, timeouts scored incorrect. Timeouts, answer-parse failures, and verified-wrong answers are scored identically as failures and are not separately logged, so timeout frequencies are not reported. The verifier therefore contributes a small downward bias to p ^ \hat{p} and q ^ \hat{q} alike; because it is applied with identical settings to both sides of every pair, it does not bias the paired difference D ⁡ ( k ) D(k) except through any differential rate of pathological outputs between base and RL models. Per-response token limits: 8k tokens ( n = 64 n=64 ) for the first pass over both pairs; 16k ( n = 256 n=256 ) for the deep ProRL and DeepScaleR comparisons; and 32k ( n = 64 n=64 ) for the conditional DeepScaleR token-limit follow-up. Truncation rates (base/RL): DeepScaleR pair at 8k: 30.6 % / 12.2 % 30.6\%/12.2\% ; ProRL pair at 8k: 30.6 % / 2.0 % 30.6\%/2.0\% ; ProRL pair at 16k: 15.5 % / 0.02 % 15.5\%/0.02\% . DeepScaleR at 32k: 5.6 % / 0.35 % 5.6\%/0.35\% . The code domain uses HumanEval+ ( 164 164 problems) and MBPP+ ( 378 378 ), 542 542 prompts in total, sampled at an 8k token limit with n = 64 n{=}64 and scored by execution: pass@ 1 1 is .221 .221 for the base, .245 .245 for DeepScaleR and .266 .266 for ProRL, so neither suite is near ceiling for these checkpoints. Domain evidence is nonetheless narrow: these are the only two code suites we ran, and the math sets are thin near p ≈ 0 p\approx 0 , which is where β tail \beta_{\mathrm{tail}} is identified. Harder suites (LiveCodeBench, Omni-MATH) would test Finding 3’s cross-domain slope stability and populate the hard tail directly; we did not run them.

Its literal-atom interpretation would require deeper sampling and decoder interventions, which are reported below.

sections.heading: The 167-prompt episode.
sections.text: The first completed sampling shard of the ProRL pair (167 prompts, 8k-token limit) showed D ^ ​ ( k ) \hat{D}(k) crossing zero at k = 18 k=18 ; the dominance test returned p = .216 p=.216 ; the completed 1000-prompt sample at the same token limit gave D ⁡ ( k ) > 0 D(k)>0 everywhere with p = .995 p=.995 . We keep the episode in the paper as a measured example of how subsample crossings arise and how the test behaves.

sections.heading: Per-slice fits (ProRL-16k).
sections.text: MATH-500 slice: EM β ^ = 1.55 \hat{\beta}=1.55 , γ ^ = 1.98 \hat{\gamma}=1.98 , π ^ 0 = .11 \hat{\pi}_{0}=.11 ; DeepScaleR-corpus slice: β ^ = 1.53 \hat{\beta}=1.53 (two-stage 0.84 0.84 ), γ ^ = 3.58 \hat{\gamma}=3.58 , π ^ 0 = .09 \hat{\pi}_{0}=.09 – .18 .18 depending on token limit. In the 8k pilot the fitted excess-zero component was 6 × 6\times higher on the MATH-500 (transfer) slice than on the corpus slice ( .145 .145 vs .024 .024 ), consistent with un-reinforced prompts drifting; the corpus slice is in-training for DeepScaleR only, and its overlap with ProRL’s multi-domain mixture is unknown, so we label the slices “transfer”/“corpus” rather than in/out-of-training for the ProRL pair.

sections.heading: DeepScaleR-32k source-specific analysis.
sections.text: The 32k sample contains 500 MATH-500 prompts and 500 prompts from the DeepScaleR corpus. We form the prompt-level contribution matrix for each source, then use independent Gaussian multipliers within source. One critical value ( 2.806 2.806 , B = 20,000 B=20{,}000 ) is the 95th percentile of the maximum absolute studentized deviation jointly over { D corpus ( k ) , D MATH ( k ) , D corpus ( k ) − D MATH ( k ) : k ≤ 64 } \{D_{\mathrm{corpus}}(k),D_{\mathrm{MATH}}(k),D_{\mathrm{corpus}}(k)-D_{\mathrm{MATH}}(k):k\leq 64\} . The corpus point estimate crosses in ( 16 , 24 ] (16,24] and the MATH-500 estimate in ( 8 , 12 ] (8,12] , but neither source-specific curve has a negative upper bound under this joint band: κ corpus ∈ [ 9 , ∞ ) \kappa_{\mathrm{corpus}}\in[9,\infty) and κ MATH ∈ [ 4 , ∞ ) \kappa_{\mathrm{MATH}}\in[4,\infty) . Unadjusted source-wise dominance p p -values are .020 .020 and .215 .215 . The global source-equality test rejects ( p < 10 − 4 p<10^{-4} ), driven chiefly by the larger small- k k improvement on the corpus slice. This post-review family is separate from the original confirmation family and is labeled as such. Figure 4: Source-specific analysis of the 32k DeepScaleR result. Left: source-specific D ⁡ ( k ) D(k) curves. Right: their contrast. Shading uses one 95% critical value jointly over both curves, the contrast, and all k k . Both point estimates cross, but neither source has a statistically supported crossing separately; only the pre-specified 50/50 mixture does.

sections.heading: Multiplicity map.
sections.text: The original public-pair discovery family contains five dominance tests and uses Holm family-wise level .05 .05 . The crossing criterion is a 95% simultaneous-over- k k statement within a pair, not a band adjusted over pair selection. DeepScaleR and 32k were selected after the 16k discovery; the 32k script and decision rule were frozen before the new counts were inspected, making this a follow-up with a pre-specified analysis conditional on the selected pair and token limit, not a confirmation on new prompts. The joint ( k , B ) (k,B) multiplier test controls search over 8k, 16k, and 32k for the selected pair; it does not control selection among the five pairs. Two independent new-prompt studies exist: the 500-fresh-prompt 16k check, whose crossing criterion and dominance endpoint both fail; and the pre-specified 1060-prompt 32k new-prompt run (Finding 2), whose crossing criterion and dominance endpoint both pass.

sections.heading: Monte Carlo stability of the 32k mixture crossing result.
sections.text: This paragraph concerns the conditional 32k mixture follow-up ( m = 1000 m{=}1000 , n = n ′ = 64 n{=}n^{\prime}{=}64 , κ ∈ [ 9 , 33 ] \kappa\in[9,33] on the dense grid), not the pre-specified fresh-prompt run of Appendix G . Because the confidence margin is small, we recomputed the simultaneous band across 20 independent multiplier draws at B = 4000 B{=}4000 : the simultaneous band endpoint at k = 48 k{=}48 has across-seed mean − 1.4 × 10 − 3 -1.4\times 10^{-3} (original single-run value − 1.6 × 10 − 3 -1.6\times 10^{-3} ) with Monte Carlo standard deviation 1.2 × 10 − 4 1.2\times 10^{-4} , and the crossing criterion holds in 20 / 20 20/20 runs (at k = 64 k{=}64 likewise 20 / 20 20/20 ; the marginal k = 32 k{=}32 cell has a negative upper bound in 1 / 20 1/20 and is not load-bearing). The crossing result is not bootstrap noise; its scientific weight is bounded instead by the effect-size reading in Finding 2.

sections.heading: Bootstrap LRT calibration (M2).
sections.text: Because the semiparametric mixture does not obviously satisfy Wilks regularity, we calibrate the likelihood-ratio test of the affine link against the monotone spline by parametric bootstrap under the fitted affine null. Observed statistics: 404 404 (DeepScaleR-16k) and 5,642 5{,}642 (ProRL-16k) against a null 95th percentile of ≈ 10 \approx 10 ( p boot = .005 p_{\mathrm{boot}}=.005 at B = 200 B=200 ).

sections.heading: Spline fallback mechanics.
sections.text: The fallback replaces the affine link by a flexible cubic spline whose truncated-power basis is exactly linear below its smallest knot, so the spline’s linear coefficient is a tail-elasticity estimate β ^ tail \hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{tail}} . This preserves within-window inference and pointwise identification of T T on the observed support; it does not automatically license tail extrapolation — below the data’s resolution ( p ≪ 1 / n p\ll 1/n ) the spline is shaped by regularization, not evidence. Under the spline, link flexibility and the latent atom compete for the same signal: π ^ 0 \hat{\pi}_{0} collapses as the spline absorbs zero-success prompts. The two are separated by exogenous variation in G G (the G G -sweep of § 6 ), not by fit alone; reassuringly, ( β ^ , γ ^ ) (\hat{\beta},\hat{\gamma}) are insensitive to the assumed G G , with the point estimate k ^ ⋆ \hat{k}^{\star} moving only within 31 31 – 35 35 over G ∈ { 4 , … , 32 } G\in\{4,\dots,32\} . This is a G G -sensitivity range for the grid-EM crossing, a different estimator from the Beta ⁡ ( a , b ) \mathrm{Beta}(a,b) -parametrized profile set [ 55 , 70 ] [55,70] reported for the same pair in Table 3 (whose own point estimate is k ^ ⋆ = 60 \hat{k}^{\star}{=}60 ); the two are not on a common scale and neither is a confidence statement about the other.

sections.heading: Knot stability (deep-sampled pairs).
sections.text: On the deep-sampled pairs ( n = 256 n{=}256 ), β ^ tail \hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{tail}} is stable across knot placements and agrees in sign with β ^ proj \hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{proj}} (DeepScaleR-16k [ 1.31 , 1.49 ] [1.31,1.49] ; ProRL-16k above 1 1 throughout but magnitude-unstable). These are deterministic-link estimates: the conditional-mean slope under a fitted dispersion family is .88 .88 and .72 .72 for the same two pairs (Table 6 ), and the two are different functionals rather than competing estimates of one exponent (§ E.2 ). At n = 64 n{=}64 it is unidentified (ranges spanning zero); for shallow-sampled runs we report β proj \beta_{\mathrm{proj}} and within-window claims only.

sections.heading: Non-invariance across checkpoints (Finding 5b).
sections.text: The one recipe available at two scales—SimpleRL-Zoo on Qwen2.5-1.5B versus Qwen2.5-Math-7B, same data, same evaluation protocol—yields non-overlapping projections: β ^ proj = 1.00 \hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{proj}}=1.00 [ 0.96 , 1.05 ] [0.96,1.05] at 1.5B versus 2.30 2.30 [ 2.11 , 2.53 ] [2.11,2.53] at 7B ( Δ scale ≈ 1.3 \Delta_{\mathrm{scale}}\approx 1.3 ). The near-location-shift operator that made SimpleRL the cleanest 1.5B row does not survive scaling. A third confound is not removable by re-measurement: the two bases differ in pretraining corpus as well as in parameter count (Qwen2.5-1.5B is general-purpose, Qwen2.5-Math-7B is math-specialized), so Δ scale \Delta_{\mathrm{scale}} confounds scale with domain pretraining on a mathematics benchmark. The 1.5B base’s failure to terminate is plausibly itself a consequence of the missing math post-training rather than of size. We therefore report Δ scale \Delta_{\mathrm{scale}} as non-invariance of the recipe-level summary across checkpoints , not as a parameter-count effect; separating the two would require a same-lineage pair at two scales, which this recipe family does not provide. Two caveats keep this descriptive: the bases truncate very differently at their shared cap ( 78 / 64 % 78/64\% at 1.5B versus 13 / 3 % 13/3\% at 7B), so scale and censoring move together; restricting to prompts where both sides truncate under 10 % 10\% leaves β ^ proj = 2.09 \hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{proj}}=2.09 at 7B, while the 1.5B pair has no such prompts—itself part of the finding. Recipe-level β \beta claims do not transfer across scale without re-measurement. A higher-token-limit re-run separates censoring from behaviour. Re-sampling the 1.5B base at 32 32 k tokens— 4 × 4\times the shared cap, all m = 1000 m{=}1000 prompts paired—moves truncation only from .784 .784 to .769 .769 (paired 95 % 95\% CI [ − .019 , − .012 ] [-.019,-.012] ) and pass@ 1 1 not at all ( .043 → .043 .043\to.043 ); no prompt clears the 10 % 10\% bar at either cap, and 362 362 of 1000 1000 truncate more at the larger one. The missing low-truncation subset is thus not purchasable: this base does not terminate, so no cap produces one, and the 1.5B row is censored by model behaviour rather than by the evaluation token limit. Our best decomposition of Δ scale ≈ 1.3 \Delta_{\mathrm{scale}}\approx 1.3 : at most ≈ 0.2 \approx 0.2 is attributable to residual censoring at 7B (the low-truncation restriction moves 2.30 2.30 only to 2.09 2.09 ), while the 1.5B side’s censoring is itself a behavioural property of the base. Most of the gap is real behaviour change — which is precisely why recipe-level language must be scale-indexed, and why we treat every scalar in Table 3 as a (checkpoint, protocol, population) property rather than a recipe constant.

sections.heading: Extended evaluation and protocol sensitivity.
sections.text: Extending the controlled evaluation to n = 256 n{=}256 per side pushes the measured sampling range from k ≤ 64 k\leq 64 to k ≤ 256 k\leq 256 : every GRPO arm’s difference curve turns negative in point estimate beyond k ≈ 128 k\approx 128 ( D ⁡ ( 256 ) = − .002 D(256)=-.002 at G = 4 G{=}4 , − .001 -.001 at G = 16 G{=}16 , − .009 -.009 at weak KL) while SFT stays positive ( + .009 +.009 ), yet none of the four runs provides statistical evidence of a crossing and none rejects dominance (weak KL comes closest, p = .20 p{=}.20 )—100 updates from this base do not buy a demonstrable inversion even at 4 × 4\times the sampling depth. Re-running the G = 4 G{=}4 pair at decoding temperature 1.0 1.0 moves the operator sharply: β ^ proj \hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{proj}} rises from 1.67 1.67 to 2.40 2.40 and γ ^ \hat{\gamma} from 2.28 2.28 to 3.65 3.65 , with base pass@1 falling .291 → .219 .291\to.219 . The operator is a property of the model-plus-decoder, not of the weights alone.

sections.heading: G G -sweep and KL sensitivity (Finding 5c).
sections.text: Completing the sweep gives β ^ proj = 1.67 , 1.68 , 1.76 \hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{proj}}=1.67,1.68,1.76 at G = 4 , 8 , 16 G=4,8,16 —a monotone but small drift whose confidence intervals overlap almost entirely, and whose extremes differ by less than the GRPO–SFT contrast by a factor of six. Under the pre-specified equivalence margin ( | Δ ​ β proj | < 0.15 |\Delta\beta_{\mathrm{proj}}|<0.15 negligible) the G = 4 G{=}4 vs G = 8 G{=}8 comparison is equivalent and the G = 4 G{=}4 vs G = 16 G{=}16 comparison is borderline, so we report group size as not a lever on the operator over this range rather than claiming a null from non-significance. The mechanical hazard factor 𝔼 ​ ( 1 − p ) G \mathbb{E}(1-p)^{G} falls with G G ( .44 → .32 → .24 .44\to.32\to.24 ), but the fitted per-encounter propensities stay near the boundary ( π ^ 0 = 0 , .008 , 0 \hat{\pi}_{0}=0,.008,0 ), giving realized masses 𝔼 ⁡ [ ρ ⁡ ( p ) ] ^ = 0 , .0027 , 0 \widehat{\mathbb{E}[\rho(p)]}=0,.0027,0 . The realized-mass sequence is therefore not monotone and does not validate M3; only its known hazard factor moves in the predicted direction. Weakening KL tenfold ( 10 − 3 → 10 − 4 10^{-3}\to 10^{-4} ) moves the shift by Δ ​ γ ^ = .026 \Delta\hat{\gamma}=.026 [ − .027 , .067 ] [-.027,.067] —directionally as γ ∼ 1 / λ \gamma\sim 1/\lambda predicts, but an effect indistinguishable from zero at our precision, and an order of magnitude smaller than the gap between training modes. The nominal KL coefficient is evidently not the theory’s λ \lambda ; the operator responds to what training is far more than to how its regularizer is dialed.

sections.heading: Affine-robust controlled shape comparison.
sections.text: For Finding 5 we additionally fit a monotone quartic Bernstein curve to η ⁡ ( x ) = logit ⁡ T ⁡ ( σ ⁡ ( x ) ) \eta(x)=\operatorname{logit}T(\sigma(x)) inside the latent-grid EM. Ordered Bernstein coefficients impose monotonicity without imposing a constant slope. The literal zero atom is fixed at zero because every controlled-run candidate revives under unrestricted decoding; continuous very-small probabilities remain available to the fit. We define the central average logit slope (integrated elasticity) β ¯ 20 : 80 = η ⁡ ( x .80 ) − η ⁡ ( x .20 ) x .80 − x .20 , x r = quantile r { logit p ~ i } , \bar{\beta}_{20:80}=\frac{\eta(x_{.80})-\eta(x_{.20})}{x_{.80}-x_{.20}},\qquad x_{r}=\operatorname{quantile}_{r}\{\operatorname{logit}\tilde{p}_{i}\}, where p ~ i = ∑ ℓ A i ​ ℓ ​ p ℓ \tilde{p}_{i}=\sum_{\ell}A_{i\ell}\,p_{\ell} is prompt i i ’s posterior-mean base difficulty under the fitted NPMLE F ^ \hat{F} (E-step weights A i ​ ℓ A_{i\ell} of Appendix C ), used so the quantiles are not driven by the raw c i / n i c_{i}/n_{i} at small counts. The functional averages the local logit slope only over observed support ( p ∈ [ .027 , .554 ] p\in[.027,.554] ), not the hardest prompts with base success probability near zero. A paired prompt bootstrap uses the same resampled indices for SFT and both GRPO runs ( B = 500 B=500 ). Estimates [95% CIs] are SFT 1.390 1.390 [ 1.278 , 1.548 ] [1.278,1.548] , GRPO G = 4 G=4 1.884 1.884 [ 1.724 , 2.253 ] [1.724,2.253] , and GRPO G = 16 G=16 1.988 1.988 [ 1.786 , 2.418 ] [1.786,2.418] ; paired differences are .495 .495 [ .281 , .861 ] [.281,.861] and .599 .599 [ .349 , 1.024 ] [.349,1.024] . The simultaneous local-slope contrast band does not exclude zero at every difficulty, so we claim an integrated central ordering, not uniform slope dominance. Crucially, SFT’s flexible-link functional is also above one: the affine “opposite sides of one” narrative is not model-robust. Figure 5 plots the fitted curves, local slopes and contrasts. The supported ordering is integrated, not pointwise over the whole range.

sections.heading: Answer-space concentration (Finding 5).
sections.text: GRPO raises the mean modal-answer share from .49 .49 to .60 .60 – .62 .62 and halves the distinct answers per prompt ( 28 → 13 28\to 13 ), while SFT lowers concentration below base ( .45 .45 ) while raising modal correctness — the answer-level mirror of the GRPO–SFT central-shape separation. The top-20 per-prompt gainers contain none of the 7 training near-duplicates: no memorization signal.

sections.heading: Repeated incorrect answers (Finding 5).
sections.text: Examining ProRL prompts with no observed successes after repeated sampling shows what the operational component captures: not degeneracy but mode lock-in — ProRL’s modal-answer share on them averages .88 .88 (several at 1.00 1.00 : a single distinct answer across all 2,304 2{,}304 draws), with zero truncation and fully formed solutions, the locked answer inheriting the base’s modal error in half the cases. The concentration that 100 GRPO updates begin ( .49 → .62 .49\to.62 ) is here taken to its fixed point. The deep-resample severity ordering (none at 100 updates; mild for DeepScaleR, ∼ \sim 1,750 steps; severe for ProRL, ∼ \sim 3,000) tracks the fitted π ^ 0 \hat{\pi}_{0} ( 0 → .08 → .23 0\to.08\to.23 ) — a dose-response in training horizon for which π ^ 0 \hat{\pi}_{0} is the severity index. Merging the standard-decoding deep resample ( 2,304 2{,}304 draws: 256 256 original + + 2,048 2{,}048 resample) with an unrestricted-decoding pass ( 2,048 2{,}048 at top- p = 1.0 p{=}1.0 ) gives 4,352 4{,}352 total generations per prompt; 13 / 22 13/22 zero-success prompts remain at zero across all decoders (binomial upper bound q < 6.9 × 10 − 4 q<6.9\times 10^{-4} (95% one-sided exact binomial)).

sections.heading: GRPO prompts with no observed successes (Finding 5).
sections.text: The four GRPO zero-success exceptions are the same two prompts in both G = 4 G{=}4 and G = 16 G{=}16 runs. On the first, the base’s modal answer ( 76 76 , the normal-approximation solution; frequency .20 .20 ) is amplified by GRPO to .36 .36 while the reference answer ( 534 534 , the Chebyshev bound; base frequency 1 / 128 1/128 ) is not observed ( 0 / 2048 0/2048 in both runs) — yet SFT, which sees the reference solution, lifts it to 32 / 2048 32/2048 . The second shows the same pattern with an arithmetic-precision error cluster ( 201 / 2048 201/2048 under SFT, 0 / 2048 0/2048 under GRPO; verifier audited on both). These cases realize the fixed-point prediction at the level of individual solution modes.

sections.heading: Prefix-rescue experiment (Finding 5).
sections.text: To distinguish opening-token routing failure from deeper reasoning inability, we gave ProRL the first { 8 , 32 , 128 , 512 , 2048 , 4096 } \{8,32,128,512,2048,4096\} tokens of a base-model correct solution as a forced prefix and let ProRL complete freely ( n = 32 n{=}32 per prompt per prefix length, temp .6 .6 , top- p p .95 .95 , 16k-token limit). Nine of the 22 ProRL zero-success prompts yielded a harvestable donor, defined before any rescue generation as a base-model completion that both verified correct and terminated naturally (untruncated) within 256 256 base draws at the 16k limit, keeping at most 3 per prompt. The remaining 13 produced no such completion and are excluded by donor availability rather than by rescue outcome; the studied nine are consequently the subset on which the base itself still succeeds, which makes the rescue rates below an upper bound on what prefix forcing achieves across all 22. Results: short prefixes are completely ineffective — 0 / 288 0/288 at 8 8 – 128 128 tokens. Rescue begins only with near-complete chains: 2 / 288 2/288 at 512 512 tokens, 6 / 256 6/256 at 2,048 2{,}048 , and 44 / 256 44/256 at 4,096 4{,}096 . Per-prompt extremes span the range: one prompt is fully rescued at 4,096 4{,}096 ( 32 / 32 32/32 ), while five prompts remain at 0 / 32 0/32 even with a 4,096 4{,}096 -token prefix. Prefix cells exist only where the donor solution is longer than the prefix, so n n falls from 9 prompts (288 completions) to 8 (256) at prefix lengths ≥ 2,048 \geq 2{,}048 : one donor solution is shorter than 2,048 2{,}048 tokens. The failure is therefore not an opening-token routing choice; the model requires most of a correct reasoning chain before recovery, and half the prompts resist rescue at every tested prefix length.

sections.heading:
Appendix E Conditional heterogeneity: the split test, refits, and the
kernel operator
sections.text: This appendix gives the full methodology and results behind § 5 . The question: given base difficulty p p , is the post-training success probability a point mass q = T ⁡ ( p ) q=T(p) (up to the zero atom), or does the conditional law H ⁡ ( q ∣ p ) H(q\mid p) carry dispersion? The distinction matters because pass@ k k depends on all conditional moments of Q | P Q\mid P : G 1 ​ ( k ∣ p ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( 1 − Q ) k ∣ p ] G_{1}(k\mid p)=\mathbb{E}[(1-Q)^{k}\mid p] , so a mean link plus atom can misplace both the fitted π 0 \pi_{0} (continuous dispersion manufactures the same excess-zero, overdispersion signal as an atom) and the model-implied crossing.

sections.heading: Design.
sections.text: Post-RL generations are split into two disjoint halves A / B A/B by generation-index parity; base generations into halves 1 / 2 1/2 . Difficulty estimates p ^ ( 1 ) , p ^ ( 2 ) \hat{p}^{(1)},\hat{p}^{(2)} come from the two base halves, so the errors-in-variables noise entering the two residuals is independent. The mean link μ ^ \hat{\mu} (isotonic regression of q ^ \hat{q} on p ^ \hat{p} , both full-sample) is cross-fitted over five prompt folds, so no prompt’s own data enters its predicted mean. Residuals r A , i = q ^ A , i − μ ^ ( − i ) ​ ( p ^ i ( 1 ) ) r_{A,i}=\hat{q}_{A,i}-\hat{\mu}^{(-i)}(\hat{p}^{(1)}_{i}) and r B , i r_{B,i} analogously. The statistic is S = m − 1 ​ ∑ i r A , i ​ r B , i S=m^{-1}\sum_{i}r_{A,i}r_{B,i} . Given ( p i , q i ) (p_{i},q_{i}) the two halves are independent, so 𝔼 ⁡ [ r A ​ r B ] ≈ 𝔼 ​ Var ​ ( Q ∣ P ) \mathbb{E}[r_{A}r_{B}]\approx\mathbb{E}\,\mathrm{Var}(Q\mid P) : binomial noise cancels across replicas and only replicable prompt-level dispersion survives.

sections.heading: Calibration.
sections.text: Writing μ ¯ ​ ( p ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ μ ^ ​ ( p ^ ( 1 ) ) ∣ p ] \bar{\mu}(p)=\mathbb{E}[\hat{\mu}(\hat{p}^{(1)})\mid p] (equal for both halves), the exact null-relevant decomposition is 𝔼 ⁡ [ r A ​ r B ] = 𝔼 ​ Var ​ ( Q ∣ P ) ⏟ target + 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( T ⁡ ( P ) − μ ¯ ​ ( P ) ) 2 ] ⏟ bias , ≥ 0 , \mathbb{E}[r_{A}r_{B}]=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\,\mathrm{Var}(Q\mid P)}_{\text{target}}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\big[(T(P)-\bar{\mu}(P))^{2}\big]}_{\text{bias},\ \geq 0}, because the two halves’ difficulty estimates are independent given p p while their cross-fitted mean-link error shares the same conditional mean. The bias term is sign-definite : the statistic’s null mean is nonnegative, so the test’s failure mode is over-rejection, never conservatism — and the term conflates mean-link misspecification with conditional dispersion, which S S alone cannot separate. We therefore never compare S S to zero. Two parametric-bootstrap nulls re-run the identical pipeline (same generation counts, same splits, same folds, including the 2 \sqrt{2} -noisier half-sample evaluation points and the within-fold dependence induced by the shared cross-fitted link, both of which the prompt-level standard error ignores) on data simulated from (a) the fitted deterministic-spline model ( π 0 = 0 \pi_{0}=0 ) and (b) the fitted zero-inflated spline model — the paper’s own fallback. Null (b) is the sharper question: the atom is prompt-level heterogeneity, so rejecting (b) provides evidence of dispersion beyond what the fitted atom explains. A real-data placebo replaces the post-RL side by two disjoint quarters of the base sample (so Q = P Q=P and the deterministic null holds exactly); its z z is within ± 2 \pm 2 for every pair. The placebo’s scope is deliberately limited: with Q = P Q=P the true mean link is the identity, which isotonic regression estimates essentially without bias, so the placebo validates the pipeline’s mechanics but cannot probe the link-misspecification component of the bias — that channel is exactly what nulls (a) and (b) calibrate. sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: (Table 5 .) Every pair rejects both nulls at the bootstrap resolution floor, with bias-adjusted z adj z_{\mathrm{adj}} between 4.5 4.5 and 9.4 9.4 . The null-mean share of S S varies enormously — 1 1 – 16 % 16\% for the public 1.5B pairs but 63 63 – 76 % 76\% for the controlled runs and the 7B pair, where the fitted deterministic-spline nulls are most contorted — which is why inference runs through the calibrated bootstrap, not through raw z z . The replicable dispersion sd ^ \widehat{\mathrm{sd}} ranges from .04 .04 (SimpleRL-Zoo) to .15 .15 (ProRL, controlled GRPO) — against per-half binomial noise of ≈ .03 \approx.03 at n ′ / 2 = 128 n^{\prime}/2=128 . The ordering is itself informative: SimpleRL-Zoo, the one pair whose affine link is not rejected and whose operator is a pure shift, has by far the smallest dispersion; the in-domain trained pairs have the largest; on code, in-domain ProRL ( .147 .147 ) exceeds transfer DeepScaleR ( .066 .066 ). Difficulty profiles differ: public 1.5B pairs concentrate dispersion on the hardest prompts (unadjusted tercile z z against zero, ordered from the lowest- p ^ \hat{p} tercile to the highest: 9.4 / 2.5 / 1.0 9.4/2.5/1.0 for DeepScaleR-16k), controlled runs on the middle ( 7.2 / 21.3 / 12.7 7.2/21.3/12.7 for G = 4 G{=}4 ), code on the easy end ( — / 2.2 / 7.4 \text{---}/2.2/7.4 for ProRL code, whose lowest- p ^ \hat{p} tercile is empty).

sections.text: Replacing the conditional point mass by Q | p ∼ Beta ⁡ ( a p , b p ) Q\mid p\sim\mathrm{Beta}(a_{p},b_{p}) with a p = T ⁡ ( p ) ​ ϕ a_{p}=T(p)\phi , b p = ( 1 − T ⁡ ( p ) ) ​ ϕ b_{p}=(1-T(p))\phi (zero atom retained) changes three formulas and nothing else. The alive-component likelihood becomes Pr ⁡ ( d ∣ p , Z = 1 ) = ( n ′ d ) ​ B ​ ( d + a p , n ′ − d + b p ) / B ⁡ ( a p , b p ) \Pr(d\mid p,Z{=}1)=\binom{n^{\prime}}{d}B(d+a_{p},\,n^{\prime}-d+b_{p})/B(a_{p},b_{p}) ; the failure moments entering model curves become 𝔼 [ ( 1 − Q ) k ∣ p , Z = 1 ] = B ( a p , b p + k ) / B ( a p , b p ) \mathbb{E}[(1-Q)^{k}\mid p,Z{=}1]=B(a_{p},\,b_{p}+k)/B(a_{p},b_{p}) (the Beta integral); and the held-out predictive uses the conjugate update Q | p , d A ∼ Beta ⁡ ( a p + d A , b p + n A − d A ) Q\mid p,d_{A}\sim\mathrm{Beta}(a_{p}+d_{A},\,b_{p}+n_{A}-d_{A}) , so p ⁡ ( d B ∣ p , d A , Z = 1 ) = ( n B d B ) ​ B ​ ( d B + a p + d A , n B − d B + b p + n A − d A ) / B ⁡ ( a p + d A , b p + n A − d A ) p(d_{B}\mid p,d_{A},Z{=}1)=\binom{n_{B}}{d_{B}}B(d_{B}+a_{p}+d_{A},\,n_{B}-d_{B}+b_{p}+n_{A}-d_{A})/B(a_{p}+d_{A},\,b_{p}+n_{A}-d_{A}) , mixed over the grid posterior of p p and the atom exactly as in the binomial case (the extinct component predicts d B = 0 d_{B}=0 ). Profiling ϕ \phi inside the grid EM gives, for the three core pairs, Table 6 (affine link; ϕ = ∞ \phi{=}\infty recovers the working model). Table 6: Beta-binomial refit: the working model ( ϕ = ∞ \phi{=}\infty ) against the same model with the conditional precision ϕ \phi profiled inside the grid EM. k ⋆ k^{\star} is the model-implied crossing under each fit; Δ ​ ℓ \Delta\ell is the log-likelihood gain from profiling ϕ \phi , computed in-sample on the full counts — not the held-out quantity of Table 8 , which carries the same symbol but scores untouched generations. ϕ = ∞ \phi=\infty (working model) ϕ \phi profiled pair β ^ \hat{\beta} π ^ 0 \hat{\pi}_{0} k ⋆ k^{\star} ϕ ^ \hat{\phi} β ^ \hat{\beta} π ^ 0 \hat{\pi}_{0} k ⋆ k^{\star} Δ ​ ℓ \Delta\ell DeepScaleR-16k 1.26 .085 36 6.5 0.88 .028 54 + 2969 +2969 ProRL-16k 1.58 .232 32 1.9 0.72 .120 80 + 6257 +6257 GRPO G = 4 G{=}4 ( n = 256 n{=}256 ) 2.08 .000 13 1.4 0.58 .000 85 + 13624 +13624 Three readings. First, the likelihood gains are enormous, and π ^ 0 \hat{\pi}_{0} falls by half to two-thirds where it was positive — direct confirmation that the working model’s atom partly absorbed continuous dispersion. Second, the surviving mean-link “ β ^ \hat{\beta} ” under dispersion is a different functional (the conditional-mean slope once the dispersion family soaks up tail behaviour) and is not a corrected sharpening exponent. This is not the two-stage attenuation of § 4 : that was a finite-count artifact within the working model, removed by the EM at no change of estimand; here the estimand itself changes with the assumed nuisance structure. Even the sign of “ β − 1 \beta-1 ” is not invariant across structures ( 1.26 → 0.88 1.26\to 0.88 ; 1.58 → 0.72 1.58\to 0.72 ), so scalar exponents are model-dependent summaries rather than primary objects: count data at these per-prompt sample sizes identify the conditional law, not a privileged scalar summary of it. Sharpening claims that survive are kernel-level — the GRPO kernels imply crossings where the SFT kernel implies none, and the within-support concentration forensics (Appendix D ) point the same way. Third, once ϕ \phi is profiled, the affine and spline links converge to nearly identical fits (ProRL: β ^ = .715 \hat{\beta}=.715 vs. .722 .722 , log-likelihoods within 2 2 nats; DeepScaleR: .88 .88 vs. .99 .99 , within 8 8 ) — much of the curvature that M2 detects is also dispersion in disguise. The beta-binomial and the kernel place k ⋆ k^{\star} differently — under the affine link of Table 6 the beta-binomial gives 54 54 and 80 80 , under the spline link used for every held-out comparison below it gives 36 36 and 80 80 (and 64 64 , 68 68 on GRPO G = 4 , 16 G{=}4,16 ), against the kernel’s 27 27 and 58 58 — so the dispersion family matters for extrapolation even though both families agree that dispersion is the finding. Which of them we report is settled in § E.3 on a held-out criterion, not by which k ⋆ k^{\star} is closer to a sample sign change. The remaining nine measured pairs behave identically (mean-link β ^ \hat{\beta} falls to .4 .4 – .9 .9 under fitted dispersion in every one; π ^ 0 \hat{\pi}_{0} moves only where it was positive; profiled ϕ ^ \hat{\phi} tracks the split test’s dispersion ordering, from 69.7 69.7 for SimpleRL-Zoo down to 1.3 1.3 for the controlled GRPO runs); full ϕ \phi profiles are in the reproducibility archive.

sections.heading: The kernel NPMLE.

Four checks bound what this does. sections.text: To separate tail sacrifice from dispersion we collapse each fitted kernel onto its own conditional mean: replace H ( ⋅ ∣ p ℓ ) H(\cdot\mid p_{\ell}) by the point mass at T ⁡ ( p ℓ ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ Q ∣ P = p ℓ ] = ∑ j w ℓ ​ j ​ q j / ∑ j w ℓ ​ j T(p_{\ell})=\mathbb{E}[Q\mid P{=}p_{\ell}]=\sum_{j}w_{\ell j}q_{j}/\sum_{j}w_{\ell j} , keep the fitted p p -marginal ∑ j w ℓ ​ j \sum_{j}w_{\ell j} , and recompute D ⁡ ( k ) = 𝔼 F ​ ( 1 − p ) k − 𝔼 F ​ ( 1 − T ⁡ ( p ) ) k D(k)=\mathbb{E}_{F}(1-p)^{k}-\mathbb{E}_{F}(1-T(p))^{k} on the integer grid k = 1 , … , 2 × 10 5 k=1,\dots,2\times 10^{5} . First, no pair keeps a crossing inside the observation window: the earliest mean-collapsed k ⋆ k^{\star} is 267 267 , an order of magnitude beyond the kernel’s 27 27 , and the controlled arms lose the crossing entirely. sections.heading: Full-data reconstruction.
sections.text: For context rather than validation, the kernel fitted to all counts reconstructs the observed sign changes where the deterministic fits do not: DeepScaleR-16k kernel k ⋆ = 27 k^{\star}{=}27 vs. observed 27 27 (zero-inflated spline: 19 19 ; affine: 36 36 ); ProRL-16k kernel 58 58 vs. observed 56 56 (zi-spline 11 11 ); GRPO G = 16 G{=}16 kernel 168 168 vs. observed ( 128,192 ] (128,192] (zi-spline 25 25 ); SFT kernel none vs. observed none ≤ 256 \leq 256 — while the zero-inflated spline fit manufactures a spurious k ⋆ = 24 k^{\star}{=}24 from its fitted atom, the mechanism § 5 warns about; SimpleRL-Zoo: none under either model, matching the data. The one miss is GRPO G = 4 G{=}4 : kernel 140 140 , above the observed ( 96,128 ] (96,128] by 9 % 9\% , against the zi-spline’s 23 23 — low by a factor of four. (GRPO crossings are quoted on an integer k k grid throughout; the coarser 400 400 -point logarithmic grid used for the beyond-window search reports the next node up, 143 143 and 170 170 .) What these comparisons recover are held-out and full-data sample trajectories of D ^ ​ ( k ) \hat{D}(k) under the fitted bivariate mixing law; they are not evidence that the corresponding population crossovers exist. By the criterion of § 2 only the 32 32 k fresh-prompt DeepScaleR crossing is statistically established: ProRL-16k ( p = .20 p{=}.20 ) and all three GRPO arms ( p ≥ .20 p\geq.20 ) are not, and the reconstructions above should be read as goodness-of-fit to a noisy statistic rather than as confirmation of a capability reversal.

sections.heading: Power reconciliation.
sections.text: Simulating the full dominance-test pipeline at m = 1000 m{=}1000 , n = n ′ = 256 n{=}n^{\prime}{=}256 from each fitted model (300 replicates; the simulation harness re-implements the test with B = 999 B{=}999 and reproduces the pre-specified pipeline’s observed p p -values within Monte Carlo error — .209 .209 vs. .20 .20 for ProRL, .036 .036 vs. .029 .029 for DeepScaleR-16k): for ProRL-16k the affine working model predicts rejection with probability .98 .98 — hard to reconcile with the observed p = .20 p{=}.20 — while the beta-binomial refit predicts .45 .45 and the kernel .22 .22 (the 1000 1000 -replicate design grid of Table 16 gives .207 .207 for the same cell): under the kernel model the observed non-rejection is the modal outcome. For DeepScaleR-16k (observed p = .029 p{=}.029 , rejected) the kernel predicts power .60 .60 ( .630 .630 on the 1000 1000 -replicate design grid of Table 16 ); rejection is unsurprising under every fit. The E0 anomaly (“power .98 .98 yet p = .20 p=.20 ”, § C ) is thereby resolved: it was a symptom of the deterministic-operator assumption, not of the test.

sections.heading: What survives.
sections.text: All within-window claims (dominance tests, crossing criteria, κ \kappa -intervals) do not depend on the response model and are unchanged. β ^ proj \hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{proj}} remains a well-defined protocol-indexed projection, but its interpretation as the exponent of a deterministic map does not survive: part of what the mean link and π ^ 0 \hat{\pi}_{0} absorb is conditional dispersion. Tail extrapolation beyond the window now carries an additional caveat: β tail \beta_{\mathrm{tail}} describes the mean of H ( ⋅ ∣ p ) H(\cdot\mid p) , and large- k k behaviour loads on the conditional law’s lower tail.

sections.text: The split test, the refits and the crossing analysis were re-run unchanged on two non-Qwen bases paired with SimpleRL-Zoo checkpoints of the same recipe, sampled with the same script, prompt population, verifier and decoding settings as the Qwen pairs ( n = n ′ = 128 n{=}n^{\prime}{=}128 , 8192 8192 tokens, T = .6 T{=}.6 , top- p p .95 .95 ).
