First, the crossing criterion is not met on either pair, with first-loss intervals κ ∈ [ 30 , ∞ ) \kappa\in[30,\infty) and [ 129 , ∞ ) [129,\infty) : within the k ≤ 128 k\leq 128 window there is no statistical evidence that the base overtakes, so these pairs speak to the operator’s form and not to crossings. Second, truncation is far heavier here than for the Qwen-1.5B pairs, because these are 7 7 – 8 8 B models held to the same 8192 8192 -token limit: 17 % / 16 % 17\%/16\% for Llama and 47 % / 39 % 47\%/39\% for DeepSeek-Math, against 0 0 – 16 % 16\% at 16k and under 1 % 1\% at 32k (§ 3 ). What matters for a paired contrast is the asymmetry, which is negligible for Llama and mild for DeepSeek-Math, and in the latter it runs against the base — the side whose advantage is not statistically established. Both pairs nonetheless measure an estimand at a lower token limit than the Qwen pairs, which is why we read them as evidence on the operator’s form rather than as comparable effect sizes. Third, the beta-binomial outscores the kernel out-of-sample on both, by roughly one standard error — the same direction as on the Qwen pairs in Table 8 . This is why the substantive claim is dispersion rather than a named dispersion family; the kernel remains the reporting model for D ⁡ ( k ) D(k) and k ⋆ k^{\star} on the held-out curve criterion of Table 9 , not because its k ⋆ k^{\star} sits closer to a sample sign change. Neither pair meets the crossing criterion, so no k ⋆ k^{\star} comparison is available here. Fourth, for both non-Qwen pairs the lowest- p ^ \hat{p} (hardest) tertile of the split summary is undefined: 41 % 41\% (DeepSeek-Math-7B) and 35 % 35\% (Llama-3.1-8B) of prompts record zero base successes, so in each case the empirical p ^ \hat{p} ties at the floor for more than a third of the sample and that tertile is empty. This affects only that descriptive breakdown; the pooled statistic and its calibration use no binning. These two pairs are also the sharpest test of the grid’s boundary treatment (§ E.2 ), since a floor this heavy is exactly where an absent p = 0 p{=}0 atom would bite: refitting both with a symmetric atom on P P leaves the model-implied crossing unmoved (Llama-3.1-8B 77 77 under either grid; DeepSeek-Math-7B none under either), and the fitted Pr ⁡ ( P = 0 ) \Pr(P{=}0) reaches only .011 .011 and .012 .012 — the NPMLE spreads zero-count base prompts across the small- p p nodes rather than banking them at the boundary. The third SimpleRL-Zoo pair in this family, Mistral-7B-v0.1, is excluded on a measurement ground rather than a resource one, and the reason is worth stating precisely because the obvious diagnosis is wrong. Under the shared protocol its post-RL checkpoint never terminates: in a 1024 1024 -generation probe every generation but 16 16 exhausted the 8192 8192 -token limit, against 30 % 30\% truncation on its own base, whose median generation is 219 219 tokens. The natural suspicion is that the answers exist but are lost, since verification parses only the last 3000 3000 characters and a looping model would push its answer out of that window. A controlled probe rejects this. Generating with the full text retained and scoring each generation twice — once on the whole text, once on the trailing window — gives identical verdicts on all 384 384 generations across both models and both stop-sequence settings: the window discards nothing, because a model that repeats “the final answer is x x ” keeps a parseable answer at the end, and a model that never finishes has none to lose anywhere. The same check clears the high-truncation pairs of Table 10 . What the probe does show is that 82 % 82\% of this checkpoint’s generations contain no \boxed expression anywhere in 8192 8192 tokens: the answer is not hidden, it is absent. Adding stop sequences ( \nQuestion: and variants) nearly doubles the verified rate, .062 → .115 .062\to.115 , yet two thirds of generations still reach the cap, so the behaviour is a genuine failure to halt rather than mere continuation into an invented next problem. A higher token limit would buy more repetition, not more terminations. The honest options are a stop-sequence change for this pair alone, which would break the protocol shared by every other pair and still leave two thirds truncated, or exclusion. We exclude it, and record the degeneration itself as the observation: RLVR on this base destroyed termination without being asked to.

sections.heading: Appendix F Re-analysis of published crossover claims
sections.text: Scope and method. We regenerated paired samples under our pre-specified protocol (§ 3 ), rather than re-using published generations. Each comparison concerns the same checkpoint, but discrepancies can reflect either inference or evaluation settings; the token-limit analyses in § 3 help distinguish them. Three caveats apply. First, our windows ( k ≤ 127 k\leq 127 or ≤ 256 \leq 256 ) do not cover every published claim: a crossover beyond the window (SimpleRL-Zoo at k ⋆ > 2 × 10 4 k^{\star}>2\times 10^{4} under the fitted model) is outside measurement range, not refuted. Second, kernel-implied power at these designs is .2 .2 – .6 .6 (§ 5 ), so non-rejection is limited evidence. Third, none of the five original positions reported uncertainty for the crossing itself; the test p p -values and k ⋆ k^{\star} sets address that gap. Thus the re-measurements do not establish the published crossover claims at their presumed strength , but do not show those claims false. checkpoint public position test p p 95% set for k ⋆ k^{\star} verdict DeepScaleR inversion-free at 8k c .029 .029 (16k) [ 20 , 43 ] [20,43] dom. rejected at 16k b ProRL boundary expansion, no inversion ( Liu et al., 2025 ) .20 .20 (16k) [ 55 , 70 ] [55,70] neither claim established SimpleRL-Zoo zero-RL family; base superiority at large k k ( Yue et al., 2025 ) 1.0 1.0 excl. k ⋆ ≤ 2 × 10 4 k^{\star}{\leq}2{\times}10^{4} no crossover ORZ zero-RL family ( Yue et al., 2025 ) 1.0 1.0 n/a a no crossing; confounded LUFFY off-policy; gains over on-policy RLVR 1.0 1.0 n/a a no crossing k ≤ 127 k{\leq}127 ; out of scope Table 11: Re-analysis of published positions (dominance test of Theorem 1 , 1000 regenerated paired prompts; Fieller sets under the working model). a Set not reported where the model is rejected (LUFFY) or the pair is token-limit-confounded (ORZ). b Not family-wise significant (Holm threshold .01 .01 ); the crossing criterion gives κ ∈ [ 14 , ∞ ) \kappa\in[14,\infty) ; the fresh-prompt confirmation failed (dominance p = .91 p=.91 ). c The public position is the absence of a reported inversion at an 8k token limit; the p = .99 p{=}.99 quoted elsewhere for this cell is our own 8k dominance test (Table 1 ), not an external claim.

sections.heading: Appendix G Pre-specified decision rules and their scope
sections.text: The following decision rules were specified before the corresponding results were examined. The 16k check used fresh prompts at the same token limit as discovery. The 32k follow-up reused the original mixture after selecting the pair and token limit from earlier results. The final 32k study instead used new prompts, with the prompt set and analysis specified before sampling. sections.heading: 32k confirmation on fresh prompts specified before sampling.
sections.text: The DeepScaleR-vs-base pair is re-measured once, at the single pre-specified per-response token limit of 32k, n = n ′ = 128 n{=}n^{\prime}{=}128 , temperature .6 .6 , top- p p .95 .95 , on a pre-specified prompt set built from OlympiadBench, Gaokao-2023-EN, AMC23 and AIME24 problems, deduplicated (exact-normalized and token-Jaccard ≥ .7 \geq.7 ) against the DeepScaleR training corpus and against every prompt used elsewhere in this paper. Primary endpoint: the crossing criterion on this population, k ≤ 128 k\leq 128 , sup- t t band at B = 4000 B{=}4000 . Secondary: the dominance test and the κ \kappa -interval. Kernel-implied power to detect a crossing under the hypothesis that the conditional 32k mixture effect transfers is .83 .83 ; under the fitted 16k fresh-prompt behaviour it is near the .05 .05 floor, so both outcomes are informative. Pre-committed treatment: if the crossing criterion is met, the result supersedes the conditional mixture result and is reported as evidence of a crossing on fresh prompts; if the criterion is not met, the paper reports that no crossing has been statistically confirmed on fresh prompts , and the 32k mixture cell is reported as mixture-specific only. Analysis code and this rule are frozen before the first fresh generation is drawn.

sections.heading: Realized outcome of the 32k new-prompt confirmation.
sections.text: Sampling completed on the pre-specified prompt set of m = 1060 m{=}1060 problems (OlympiadBench 633 633 , Gaokao-2023-EN 358 358 , AMC23 39 39 , AIME24 30 30 ) with n = n ′ = 128 n{=}n^{\prime}{=}128 throughout. The crossing criterion was evaluated by the frozen script with only the pair table and the output path changed; the bootstrap size, level, k k -grid and band construction are byte-identical to the code used for every other pair. Primary endpoint: pass. On the frozen sparse grid the sup- t t band has L ⁡ ( k ) > 0 L(k)>0 for k ≤ 8 k\leq 8 and U ⁡ ( k ) < 0 U(k)<0 for k ≥ 64 k\geq 64 , so the crossing criterion holds and the pre-registered first-loss budget is κ ∈ [ 9 , 64 ] \kappa\in[9,64] (Table 14 ; the dense-grid restatement is κ ∈ [ 11 , 61 ] \kappa\in[11,61] , see Post hoc grid densification below). Secondary: the dominance test gives p = .0027 p{=}.0027 , below the .01 .01 Holm threshold used elsewhere, and the κ \kappa -interval is as above. The confidence margins are δ + = .0655 \delta_{+}{=}.0655 at k = 1 k{=}1 and δ − = 3.7 × 10 − 3 \delta_{-}{=}3.7\times 10^{-3} at k = 128 k{=}128 ; the point estimates at those sampling budgets k k are + .076 +.076 and − .020 -.020 . Stability and scope. Repeating the multiplier bootstrap under 20 20 independent seeds supports the crossing in 20 / 20 20/20 , with κ = [ 9 , 64 ] \kappa=[9,64] in every sparse-grid replicate and κ = [ 11 , 60 ] \kappa=[11,60] – [ 11 , 63 ] [11,63] on the dense grid (lower endpoint 11 11 in 20 / 20 20/20 ). Per-source analyses were not pre-specified and are descriptive only: OlympiadBench ( m = 633 m{=}633 ) meets the crossing criterion with κ = [ 10 , 69 ] \kappa=[10,69] , Gaokao-2023-EN ( m = 358 m{=}358 ) does not ( κ ∈ [ 7 , ∞ ) \kappa\in[7,\infty) , dominance p = .12 p{=}.12 ; its point estimate first turns negative at k = 11 k{=}11 ). Truncation is 7.8 % 7.8\% on the base side and 0.7 % 0.7\% post-RL. The scorer evaluates correctness independently of the length stop: a truncated generation can already contain a correct answer. The following analysis therefore changes only generations that both truncated and were scored incorrect.

sections.heading: Post hoc grid densification.
sections.text: The pre-registered analysis evaluated the band on the frozen sparse grid { 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 6 , 8 , 12 , 16 , 24 , 32 , 48 , 64 , 96 , 128 } \{1,2,3,4,6,8,12,16,24,32,48,64,96,128\} , which certifies the crossing with κ ∈ [ 9 , 64 ] \kappa\in[9,64] . Proposition 1 states the first-loss interval over all integers k ≤ K k\leq K , and a sparse grid bounds the first loss only at the grid points it contains, so after the fact we recomputed every band in this paper on the dense grid k = 1 , … , K k=1,\dots,K with the same data, B B , level and construction ( --ks dense in pilot/certificate.py ). Densifying raises the sup- t t critical value by less than 10 − 3 10^{-3} ( 2.5422 → 2.5423 2.5422\to 2.5423 here) and the crossing criterion is unchanged. The dominance statistic of Theorem 1 is a minimum over all k ≤ K k\leq K , so the dense grid is its faithful evaluation; recomputed there it gives p = .0025 p{=}.0025 against the pre-registered p = .0027 p{=}.0027 , a difference of one bootstrap draw at B = 4000 B{=}4000 . We report the pre-registered value throughout. For the band: L ⁡ ( k ) > 0 L(k)>0 now for all k ≤ 10 k\leq 10 and U ⁡ ( k ) < 0 U(k)<0 for all k ≥ 61 k\geq 61 , giving κ ∈ [ 11 , 61 ] \kappa\in[11,61] . Only the scope of the statement changes — the first loss is now excluded at every integer below the interval, not only at the grid points — and the interval is strictly contained in the pre-registered one. Tables 1 and 14 report the dense values. No qualitative conclusion in the paper depends on the choice of grid: every pair in Table 1 keeps its crossing verdict, and every first-loss interval in this paper either is unchanged or moves inward (the non-Qwen SimpleRL pairs move [ 25 , ∞ ) → [ 30 , ∞ ) [25,\infty)\to[30,\infty) for SimpleRL Llama-3.1-8B and stay at [ 129 , ∞ ) [129,\infty) for SimpleRL DeepSeek-Math-7B; in Table 1 , DeepScaleR 8k [ 25 , ∞ ) → [ 28 , ∞ ) [25,\infty)\to[28,\infty) , 16k [ 13 , ∞ ) → [ 14 , ∞ ) [13,\infty)\to[14,\infty) , 16k fresh [ 9 , ∞ ) [9,\infty) unchanged, 32k mixture [ 9 , 48 ] → [ 9 , 33 ] [9,48]\to[9,33] , ProRL 16k [ 17 , ∞ ) → [ 24 , ∞ ) [17,\infty)\to[24,\infty) , LUFFY [ 97 , ∞ ) → [ 109 , ∞ ) [97,\infty)\to[109,\infty) , ORZ and SimpleRL-Zoo [ 129 , ∞ ) [129,\infty) unchanged). With the per-generation bits recovered for the full population, the split-generation test runs on this pre-specified fresh sample as well and rejects determinism again: z = 9.8 z{=}9.8 with calibrated p ≤ .0025 p\leq.0025 , against a base-quarters placebo of 1.9 1.9 and a residual dispersion sd ^ = .095 \widehat{\mathrm{sd}}{=}.095 . The outcome is the one the kernel favoured, and the two new-prompt experiments are consistent with it rather than with each other’s surface reading: the 16k fresh test failed ( p = .91 p{=}.91 ) under a sampling design where the same kernel put power near .05 .05 . sections.heading: Appendix H Power of the dominance test at shallow crossings

Some crossings are out of reach : the G = 4 G{=}4 arm never reaches .80 .80 on the grid, and even a 3.3 × 10 7 3.3\times 10^{7} -generation design gives power only .060 .060 . text: RLVR is a Kernel, Not a Function: Statistical Inference for pass@𝑘 Crossovers Skip to main content Report GitHub Issue × Title: Content selection saved. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2609.22547v1 [stat.ML] 18 Sep 2026 RLVR is a Kernel, Not a Function: Statistical Inference for pass@ k k Crossovers Chen Yang Affiliation: Department of Statistics, Texas A&M University Xianyang Zhang Affiliation: Department of Statistics, Texas A&M University Jun Chen Affiliation: Division of Computational BiologyDepartment of Quantitative Health Sciences, Mayo Clinic * Corresponding authors: zhangxiany@stat.tamu.edu , Chen.Jun2@mayo.edu Abstract Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) often improves pass@1 while falling behind its base model at larger sampling budgets k k , a crossover read as evidence that RLVR only sharpens existing capability. We identify two limits to this reading. First, a visible crossing need not be statistically established: comparing models on the same prompts, we build confidence bands across sampling budgets k k that require evidence of both an early gain and a later loss. Across five public RLVR pairs no crossing is statistically established in the initial evaluations, while a 32k-token evaluation on fresh prompts locates a reversal with first loss between 11 and 61 samples; power analysis shows why failure to detect a crossing need not mean no crossing, and why more prompts can help more than more answers per prompt. Second, base success alone does not determine what RLVR does to a prompt: prompts with the same base success rate have different post-RL success rates, and these differences repeat across independent generation halves. The relationship is a conditional distribution—a Markov kernel—rather than a single curve, and fitting it predicts crossings in independent generations for the same prompts and corrects the simple model’s power estimates. Theory further shows how losses on a minority of the hardest prompts can overturn an early lead even when training improves other prompts, separating evidence that a crossover exists from claims about what it means for capability. 1 Introduction The RLVR-capability debate asks whether reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards teaches a model anything its base could not already do. Since Yue et al. (2025) its central evidence has been a picture: the RL model wins at pass@1, the base wins at pass@256, and the curves cross in between — read as sharpening by one camp ( Yue et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) and contested on metric or horizon by the other ( Wen et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . Where uncertainty is quantified at all, it is per- k k intervals against seed noise ( Zhou, 2026b ; Strozzi, 2026 ) . The missing object is paired inference across sampling budgets: a confidence-band criterion that tests whether an observed crossing is statistically supported and bounds where it occurs. How much can go wrong? Three examples from 1000 paired prompts. Crossings appear in subsamples : a 167-prompt shard of ProRL/base crossed at k = 18 k{=}18 ; the full sample overturned it. Crossings can be insignificant at very large sample sizes : ProRL’s crossing at k = 56 k{=}56 is not statistically established at 1000 × 256 1000{\times}256 generations ( p = .20 p{=}.20 ). And the comparison depends on the per-response token limit : DeepScaleR shows no crossing at 8k, yet at 16k the point estimate changes sign at k = 27 k{=}27 and the dominance test rejects unadjusted ( p = .029 p{=}.029 , not family-wise significant across the five-pair discovery family); the crossing criterion, which requires statistical evidence of a gain and a loss, passes only at 32k (Figure 1 ). The crossover lives at the edge of detectability and moves with measurement choices that routinely go unreported. Figure 1: Four claims, not one: effects of the token limit. DeepScaleR vs. its base, 1000 mixture prompts, three per-response token limits: D ^ ​ ( k ) \hat{D}(k) with 95% pointwise and simultaneous (sup- t t ) bounds L ⁡ ( k ) , U ⁡ ( k ) L(k),U(k) ; the strip colours each k k by the strongest supported claim. A visual sign change appears at 16k, dominance is rejected at 16k and 32k, and a statistically supported sign change (dark-red cell) exists only at 32k; the new-prompt confirmation is in Table 1 . We study the paired difference D ⁡ ( k ) = pass@ ​ k RL − pass@ ​ k base D(k)=\text{pass@}k^{\mathrm{RL}}-\text{pass@}k^{\mathrm{base}} : paired inference tests for crossings (§ 2 ), while a response model explains their shape (§ 4 ). A 32k evaluation on fresh prompts confirms a crossing. Non-detection elsewhere must be read alongside power: under the fitted kernels, dominance-test power is .2 .2 – .6 .6 for the two public pairs (§ 3 ). The main lesson comes after that calibration. Even for a fixed model pair, prompts with the same base success probability p p can have different post-training probabilities q q , and a split-generation test shows these differences repeat beyond sampling noise. So p ↦ q p\mapsto q is not a single curve: we need the distribution of q q among prompts sharing p p , a Markov kernel (§ 5 ). This matters because pass@ k k depends nonlinearly on success probability, so the mean response to training does not determine the whole pass@ k k curve. Contributions. 1. Paired inference and empirical evaluation (§ 2 – 3 ): simultaneous bands for the paired difference curve, a dominance test, and a crossing criterion with a first-loss interval (Proposition 1 ), valid without an operator model. No public pair meets it in the initial evaluations; a 32k-token re-measurement on fresh prompts does, locating the first loss between k = 11 k{=}11 and k = 61 k{=}61 . 2. Yue et al. (2025) established the crossover across six RLVR algorithms and read it as evidence that RLVR does not exceed the base; Wen et al. (2026) credit intermediate reasoning (CoT-Pass@K); Wu et al. (2025) characterize RLVR as support-constrained conservative reweighting, the mechanism closest to ours; Liu et al. (2025) argue prolonged training expands the boundary. Zhou (2026b) and Strozzi (2026) attach seed-level intervals to crossovers; Kim et al. (2025) bin post-RL gains by base success rate, the descriptive precursor of our fitted map. All treat the effect as a deterministic map on prompt-level success rates ( Fan et al., 2026 , also) , the assumption § 5 rejects. Clay et al. (2026) manipulate base probabilities, rewards, and training prompts in controlled tasks, showing that dense rewards can overcome sparse-reward failures for behaviors with low initial probability. These interventions complement our paired inference: a crossover alone does not identify a learning mechanism, and low initial probability is not absence from the base distribution. Statistical treatments of pass@ k k . Kazdan et al. (2025) extrapolate pass@ k k within one model by beta-binomial fit; we adopt their estimator as our base stage. Levi (2026) is the closest theory: in a solvable supervised model the pass@ k k exponent rises with data, where our mechanism predicts reward-driven redistribution that flattens it ( a ↦ a / β tail a\mapsto a/\beta_{\mathrm{tail}} ); Finding 5 tests the within-support direction. Repeated-sampling scaling originates with Brown et al. (2024) , its power laws derived from difficulty heterogeneity by Schaeffer et al. (2025) . Hariri et al. (2026) replace pass@ k k with a single-model posterior and Dragoi et al. (2025) show pass@ k → 1 k\to 1 by guessing; Miller (2024) ; Bowyer et al. (2025) treat error bars for scalar accuracy, Bay & Yearick (2026) model the within-prompt correlation our bootstrap exploits, and Zhou (2026a) propose four tail-exponent checks that we adopt. Hazard-curve crossing procedures exist ( Cheng et al., 2009 ) but assume independent arms. Exponential tilting. Huang et al. (2024) characterize KL-regularized RL as an exponential tilt, and GX-Chen et al. (2025) , Mroueh (2025) , Polson et al. (2026) and Tomihari & Sato (2026) give variational, Bayesian, and distillation views of the same structure. All characterize the optimal policy form; we take the tilt as given and study the paired comparison and its statistical structure. 8 Discussion A visible crossover need not be statistically established, and failure to detect one need not mean absence; paired bands and power analysis separate these claims. The kernel result explains why base success alone is insufficient: prompts at the same p p respond differently to training, so a fitted slope summarizes but does not replace that distribution, and extrapolation beyond the measured range requires checking H ⁡ ( q ∣ p ) H(q\mid p) . A reporting protocol. Four recommendations follow. 1. Check truncation and token-limit sensitivity. Report truncation on both sides and whether raising the limit changes the comparison; distinguish observed outcomes from hypothetical repairs. 2. Consider more prompts before deeper sampling. Choose n n to cover the target sampling budgets k ≤ n k\leq n , then assess the power gained by spending on more prompts. Pooling benchmarks changes the target population (Appendix H ). 3. Use simultaneous bands when searching across k k . A crossing requires a gain at smaller k k and a loss at larger k k (Proposition 1 ); rejecting dominance alone does not establish it, though pointwise intervals remain appropriate at a single pre-specified k k . 4. Run the split-generation check before quoting an exponent. It needs no extra sampling, and replicable residual covariance means a fitted slope summarizes a distribution of responses, not a single curve. Limitations. The crossing is confirmed on fresh prompts, but its late-loss margin at 32k is small. Kernel validation holds out generations, not prompts; the non-Qwen and scale checks support the dispersion diagnostic without replicating effect sizes, and the single two-scale comparison confounds parameter count with math-specialized pretraining. Beyond-window quantities ( k ⋆ k^{\star} , confidence sets) are fitted-law extrapolations, so safety readings at large k k are questions the framework can pose, not conclusions established here. Domain evidence is narrow (Appendix D ). Ethics statement This work analyzes publicly released model checkpoints on public benchmark problems and introduces no new data collection involving human subjects. Improved statistical rigor for pass@ k k claims bears on safety evaluation, where overconfident “safe at k = 1 k=1 ” claims can mask large- k k risk. Reproducibility statement All sampling configurations (decoding parameters, per-response token limits, verifier), per-prompt counts, per-generation correctness bits (used by the split-generation test), fitted objects, and the estimation/inference/heterogeneity code ( passk-inference ) accompany the submission as an anonymized supplementary archive, together with the pre-specified model checks M1–M3, the tail-exponent checks, and the decision rules and realized outcomes of Appendix G . A public repository link will be provided at camera-ready. AI use statement Large language models were used as coding and writing assistants throughout this project: drafting and refactoring analysis code, managing compute jobs, literature search, and prose editing, all under author direction and review. The theoretical results, experimental design, and interpretation were verified by the authors; all numerical claims trace to released code and per-prompt counts.
